docs.title: SPieGeL
docs.text:
SPieGeL is an open-source, configurable Linked Data publishing server. Every resource is served in the representation the client asks for: HTML for people, and Turtle, RDF/XML, N-Triples or JSON-LD for machines.

Spiegel is Dutch for mirror. A mirror shows the same thing in a different form, which is what content negotiation does for a resource on /doc/ and /ns/. The capitals honour the founders (Stijn, Pieter and Geert), and the L stands for Linked Data.

Status

Early design phase. Nothing is ready for use yet.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Analysis: why SPieGeL exists, what its predecessor does, what SPieGeL must do, and how it compares with existing tools.
  • Architecture decisions: the decisions taken so far, and why.
  • Source code on GitHub.

docs.title: Architecture decision records
docs.text:
An architecture decision record (ADR) captures one significant decision: its context, the decision itself and its consequences. ADRs are numbered and never deleted. A decision that is reversed gets a new ADR that supersedes the old one.

Use template.md for new records.

No. Title Status 0001 Record architecture decisions Accepted 0002 Documentation as Markdown, published with MkDocs Accepted 0003 Build with the departmental Jenkins Accepted 0004 Technology baseline Accepted 0005 Use the Flux design system for HTML Accepted 0006 Publish resources and event streams as complementary forms Accepted 0007 Use the URI as the shared identifier in every distribution Accepted 0008 Do not use Neo4j as a data source for SPieGeL Accepted 0009 Translate relational sources with Ontop, materialise other sources with RML Accepted 0010 Use Jena's graph types in the core, keep SPARQL out of it Accepted 0011 Check every query against a query policy before it runs Accepted 0012 Describe tenants in RDF, with one generic template and exceptions Accepted 0013 Deliver tenant configuration as a versioned artefact Accepted 0014 Keep Linked-Data-specific components in SPieGeL, contribute generic ones to Flux Accepted 0015 Serve large and follow-up data as paged Hydra lists Accepted 0016 Answer errors to machines with problem details (RFC 9457) Accepted 0017 Serve framed JSON-LD with a generated, frozen context Accepted 0018 Minimise personal data from requests; leave personal data in the data to the store Accepted 0019 Advertise entry points to search engines, with schema.org for datasets and terms Accepted 0020 Key the cache by profile, and tag responses with data and configuration version Accepted 0021 Take labels of external vocabularies from reviewed extracts in the configuration Accepted 0022 Keep TLS and flood protection at the edge; move the 303, CORS and real rate limits into SPieGeL Accepted 0023 Link resources to their event streams from configuration, and serve versions as ordinary resources Accepted 0024 Compact JSON-LD from CONSTRUCT and DESCRIBE with the tenant's context, unless another form is asked for Accepted 0025 Offer federated queries in the portal, run by Comunica in the visitor's browser Accepted 0026 Draw SPieGeL's boundary by what answers requests, what runs in CI, what holds data, and what runs at the consumer Accepted

docs.title: 0001. Record architecture decisions
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-01

docs.title: Context
docs.text: SPieGeL replaces a platform whose design decisions were largely implicit: spread over scripts, templates and deployment configuration, and often only recoverable by reading code. As an open-source project, SPieGeL will also have contributors who were not present when decisions were taken.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We record every architecturally significant decision as an ADR in docs/adr/, following Michael Nygard's format. The analysis is a snapshot that informs decisions; ADRs are where decisions are made.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Open questions in the analysis are closed by an ADR, which the question then links to.
  • Reversing a decision means writing a new ADR, so the history stays readable.

docs.title: 0002. Documentation as Markdown, published with MkDocs
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-01

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The analysis that preceded SPieGeL was written as self-contained HTML files. That works for an internal snapshot, but not for an open-source project: HTML is hard to review in pull requests, GitHub does not render it, and external contributors expect plain text.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• All documentation is Markdown under docs/, written in British English.
  • Diagrams use Mermaid, which renders both on GitHub and on the documentation site.
  • The documentation site is built with MkDocs and the Material theme, and published on GitHub Pages at https://milieuinfo.github.io/SPieGeL/.
  • The build runs with --strict, so broken links fail the build.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One source serves both the repository view and the site.
  • The documentation toolchain needs Python. That is acceptable because it runs only in CI and on writers' machines, not in the product.
  • MkDocs is pinned below 2.0 (requirements-docs.txt). The Material team warns that MkDocs 2.0 removes the plug-in and theming systems that Material depends on. Before lifting the pin, we will review the options again, for example a successor to Material or another generator.
  • A formal specification (for example of the configuration format) may later need a W3C-style tool such as ReSpec. That would be a separate decision.

docs.title: 0003. Build with the departmental Jenkins
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-01

docs.title: Context
docs.text: SPieGeL is hosted on GitHub but built and released by the Department of Environment and Spatial Development. The department's other public repositories on GitHub are built by its own Jenkins, using a shared pipeline library. That library covers Maven builds, releases, static analysis and vulnerability scanning. Some of these repositories also publish GitHub Pages from Jenkins.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• SPieGeL is built by the departmental Jenkins with the shared pipeline library, through Jenkinsfile.groovy in the repository root.
  • The pipeline builds the documentation with MkDocs and, on the main branch, pushes the result to the gh-pages branch.
  • No GitHub Actions workflows for now.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Builds, releases and scans follow the same process as the department's other projects.
  • Pull requests from external forks are not built automatically, because untrusted code must not run on internal infrastructure, and contributors cannot see internal build results. When external contributions start, a minimal public CI for forks will be reconsidered (see Open questions).

docs.title: 0004. Technology baseline
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-01

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The analysis proposes a Maven multi-module build in a hexagonal layout. Before the first line of code, we fix the build coordinates and the main technology versions, so that every module starts from the same base.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Item Choice Group identifier be.vlaanderen.omgeving.spiegel (in line with other departmental projects, such as be.vlaanderen.omgeving:oddtoolkit) Artefact identifiers spiegel-parent, spiegel-core, spiegel-adapter-*, spiegel-app Java 21 (LTS) as the compilation target. The build also runs on newer JDKs, including the JDK 25 used in CI. Spring Boot 4.1.x, through spring-boot-starter-parent. Only spiegel-app and inbound web adapters depend on Spring. Apache Jena 6.2.x, for the SPARQL adapter. Tests JUnit 5 and AssertJ. ArchUnit enforces the dependency rules. Versioning Semantic versioning; tags v{version} through the Maven release plugin. Artefacts Published to the departmental Artifactory, like other departmental projects.

Modules are added when they are needed. Phase 1 starts with spiegel-core, spiegel-adapter-config, spiegel-adapter-sparql, spiegel-adapter-web, spiegel-adapter-html and spiegel-app. spiegel-adapter-security follows in a later phase.

Amended on 2026-10-05: the module for non-RDF sources was called spiegel-adapter-r2rml. It is renamed spiegel-adapter-rml, because RML generalises R2RML (see FR-DS-02). The module did not exist yet, so nothing else changed.

Amended on 2026-10-25: there is no module for non-RDF sources. Relational sources are read through spiegel-adapter-sparql from an Ontop endpoint, and other sources are materialised in the loading chain (ADR 0009).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• spiegel-core inherits Spring Boot's plug-in and dependency management through the parent POM, but has no Spring dependency. ArchitectureTest checks this on every build.
  • Raising the Java target to 25 is a separate, later decision, once every build and run environment supports it.
  • The Maven enforcer plug-in requires Maven 3.8.7 or later and Java 21 or later. It does not enforce dependency convergence: Jena and Spring Boot pull in slightly different versions of shared libraries, and strict convergence would break on every upgrade.

docs.title: 0005. Use the Flux design system for HTML
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-04

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
SPieGeL serves HTML subject pages, vocabulary pages, a front page per domain and an HTML view of SPARQL results. The predecessor renders them with XSLT and the Vue 2 components of omgeving-ld, which are not part of any design system. The Flemish Government's house style is turned into web components by the department's Flux team. New applications of the department are expected to use Flux, which also brings guidelines on accessibility and Content Security Policy.

The choice was left open in the analysis (open question 9). See Design system: Flux for what Flux offers and how it maps onto the predecessor.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
SPieGeL's HTML complies with the Flux design system, version 2 (2.20.0 at the time of writing), and follows its upgrades:

  • Pages follow Flux's page-layout pattern and use Flux components and styles wherever one exists, preferring the next variants and avoiding deprecated components.
  • Linked-Data-specific components that Flux lacks are built to Flux's conventions: Lit elements, CSS-in-JS with Flux's CSS variables, CSP-compliant, WCAG AA, with component and accessibility tests.
  • The omgeving-ld components are not carried over.

The choice of template engine remains open.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• spiegel-adapter-html needs a front-end build (Node.js, pnpm, a bundler) that produces a bundle of the Flux components SPieGeL uses and of its own components. That build must run in Maven and in Jenkins, with read access to the department's Artifactory for the @domg-wc packages.
  • Several components have to be built: a resource description, a hierarchy tree, incoming relations, a collection table, a geometry map and a SPARQL editor. That is work the predecessor did not need to do again.
  • Accessibility (NFR-UI-02) and a strict Content Security Policy (NFR-UI-03) become testable requirements.
  • SPieGeL depends on Flux's release cycle, including the planned v3. Its licence and availability to external contributors are still to be clarified (open question 22).
  • Pages that rely on the old components' conventions (ld-subject, browser-side .rq templates) will no longer get them. Whether those conventions must stay for a transition period is open question 8.

docs.title: 0006. Publish resources and event streams as complementary forms
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-06

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The department publishes Linked Data in two ways. Resource endpoints answer a request for one URI with the current description of that resource: that is SPieGeL's job. Linked Data Event Streams (LDES) publish every change to a collection of resources as an append-only stream that clients can replicate and keep in sync. The department leads the OpenLDES project, which builds an LDES server and client components (LDIO), and intends to make LDES a real part of its publication.

Both forms need one information architecture. Without it, each domain decides for itself how much of the surrounding graph a description contains. That makes descriptions unpredictable in size, duplicates data across endpoints and streams, and leaves consumers unsure where the authoritative description of a resource lives.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Two forms of the same data. Resource endpoints and event streams publish the same resources, with the same URIs and the same application profiles (OSLO, SHACL shapes). A resource endpoint serves a resource's current state; an event stream serves its history and lets a consumer replicate it.
  2. A description is bounded to its subject. It holds the subject's own properties. An object that is itself a resource appears by its IRI only: it is described at its own endpoint or in its own stream. There are two exceptions:
    • the label (and, where needed, the type) of a linked resource, so that it can be presented without a further request (FR-HTML-10);
    • values without an identity of their own, such as a measurement with its unit, published as a blank node or a Skolem IRI (FR-RA-04, FR-URI-04).
  3. Integration happens on the consumer's side. A consumer that needs more than one resource combines the data itself: by dereferencing the IRIs it finds, by replicating several streams with an LDES client and joining them, or by querying a domain's SPARQL endpoint. SPieGeL does not join data across domains on the consumer's behalf, and its /sparql refuses SERVICE (ADR 0011), so a federated query runs in the consumer's own query engine.
  4. SPieGeL does not serve event streams. Streams are served by an LDES server, such as OpenLDES's. SPieGeL makes them discoverable from the domains it publishes.
  5. Streams may feed SPieGeL's stores. An LDES client that materialises a stream into a store (for example LDIO) is a valid part of the loading chain (open question 15). It also fits the derived public stores of open question 29.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Descriptions have a predictable size, and their queries become simpler: they select the subject's own triples plus the agreed exceptions. This limits, but does not remove, the risk of very large resources: a subject can still have many values for one property. Such properties are paged (FR-RA-07), and every description has a ceiling on its size (NFR-OPS-09).
  • Incoming relations are not part of a description. The HTML view shows them through follow-up requests (FR-HTML-05). An RDF client finds them through SPARQL or by replicating the stream that holds them.
  • Consumers make more requests, or run an LDES client, to assemble a larger dataset. That is the intended division of work, and it is cacheable on both sides.
  • The state that SPieGeL serves must equal the latest state in the stream. Both forms must therefore come from the same source and the same shapes. Whether SPieGeL also serves version objects and past states is open question 30.
  • Discovery between both forms needs a convention: from a domain to its streams, and from a resource to the stream that publishes it (FR-ES-01, open question 30).
  • Integration across stores and domains on the consumer's side, for example with a federating query engine such as Comunica, is left for later (open question 31).

docs.title: 0007. Use the URI as the shared identifier in every distribution
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-06

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The same things are published in several forms. Besides SPieGeL's resource endpoints and event streams (ADR 0006), a river segment may also be a feature in an OGC API Features collection or a WFS layer, a row in a CSV download, or a record in a business API. Each form tends to have its own local identifier. A user who finds a segment in a map viewer then has no way to reach everything else that is known about it, and a consumer cannot join the forms without a lookup table.

The W3C Spatial Data on the Web Best Practices recommend globally unique, persistent HTTP URIs for spatial things (Best Practice 1), and linking resources together (Best Practice 3).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. The id URI is the identifier of a thing in every form in which it is distributed, not only in Linked Data. A GIS layer, a download or an API carries the thing's URI, for example as an attribute of each feature, next to any local identifier it needs.
  2. Any application that shows a thing can act as a portal. A map viewer, a dashboard or a spreadsheet links to the URI. Following that link in a browser leads, through the 303 redirect, to SPieGeL's subject page, with more information and links to related resources.
  3. SPieGeL's subject page is the landing page for such links, and can link back to the thing in the other forms, for example to the feature in an OGC API or to a map viewer centred on it (FR-HTML-13).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• SPieGeL's subject pages must work as landing pages for users who arrive from elsewhere: HTML by default for a browser (FR-CN-08), readable without JavaScript (NFR-UI-04), and with the URI policy kept stable (NFR-OPEN-02).
  • Data owners must add the URI to their other distributions. That is work outside SPieGeL, and it needs a shared convention: the attribute name, and how a feature links to its URI. GML is a constraint: a gml:id must be an XML name and cannot hold a URI, so the URI goes into an attribute. Where the convention is documented and who owns it is open question 32.
  • Joining data across forms becomes a matter of matching URIs, without lookup tables.
  • A URI that is published in a GIS layer is as hard to change as one published in Linked Data. NFR-OPEN-02 applies to it as well.

docs.title: 0008. Do not use Neo4j as a data source for SPieGeL
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Neo4j is a property graph database, queried with Cypher. It is strong at traversals and graph algorithms, and has its own full-text and vector indexes. It was raised as a possible store for some of the department's use cases. The question is whether SPieGeL should be able to read from it. The full analysis is open question 33.

SPieGeL is built on SPARQL. Data sources are SPARQL endpoints (FR-DS-01), queries are .rq files under version control (FR-RA-02), and every domain offers a public SPARQL 1.1 endpoint (FR-SPARQL-01, FR-SPARQL-02). Neo4j has no SPARQL. A tenant on Neo4j would therefore still need a triple store for /sparql, and would maintain its queries in two languages. The data source port also returns RDF, as Jena graphs (ADR 0010), so a Cypher adapter would have to translate property graph results back to RDF.

RDF reaches Neo4j through the neosemantics plugin (n10s), a Neo4j Labs project that is not a supported product and does not run on the Aura cloud service. By default it keeps triples but not their named graph. Language tags, datatypes, blank nodes and Skolem IRIs, which SPieGeL relies on (FR-HTML-10, FR-URI-04, FR-RA-04), have to be imitated in the property graph.

SPieGeL's access levels rest on named graphs: each level's store account can only read that level's graphs (NFR-SEC-02), and access is restricted per triple (open question 29). Neo4j's fine-grained permissions apply to labels, relationship types and properties, and as far as we know only in the commercial Enterprise edition. Using them would mean a new security design.

Neo4j's strengths add little to SPieGeL's own task. Keyword search uses the data source's full-text index (FR-SRCH-01), hierarchies and collections work with SPARQL property paths (FR-HTML-05), and a description is bounded to its subject (FR-RA-06), so deep traversals are not needed.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Neo4j is not a data source for SPieGeL. SPieGeL gets no Cypher adapter behind its data source port, and tenants keep their data in SPARQL stores.
  2. Neo4j may be used beside SPieGeL, for use cases where a property graph is stronger than SPARQL, such as network analysis, graph data science, visual exploration or GraphRAG. In that case:
    • the loading chain builds a Neo4j database from an explicit allowlist of public graphs, as a derived artefact like an HDT file or a QLever index (option 4 of open question 29); or
    • a source system that already keeps its data in Neo4j exports it to RDF, which is loaded into the triple store like the materialised sources of open question 28.
  3. Nodes keep the things' URIs, so that an application built on Neo4j links back to SPieGeL's subject pages (ADR 0007).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• SPieGeL keeps one query language, one result model and one security model. No round trip RDF → Neo4j → RDF has to be proven lossless or kept under test.
  • Every tenant needs a SPARQL store. Data that lives only in Neo4j must be exported to RDF before SPieGeL can publish it, so it is not live.
  • A Neo4j database built by the loading chain holds public data only. The security boundary stays in the loading chain, and Neo4j's permissions do not have to replicate the access levels.
  • Building and running such a database is a matter for the loading chain (open question 15) and for the consumer application (ADR 0006), not for SPieGeL.
  • Which use cases actually need Neo4j remains open (open question 33). If one ever requires SPieGeL to read live data from Neo4j, a new ADR must supersede this one.

docs.title: 0009. Translate relational sources with Ontop, materialise other sources with RML
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-25

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
FR-DS-02 asks that non-RDF sources can be published through declarative mappings: relational databases (for example PostgreSQL and Trino), and files or Web APIs in CSV, JSON or XML. The analysis so far assumed that SPieGeL would read them through an RML adapter (spiegel-adapter-rml, ADR 0004) behind its data source port, and drew an "RML data source" in the hexagonal design.

That adapter does not fit the tools. Open question 28 compared them:

  • Every RML processor we looked at (RMLMapper, RMLStreamer, CARML, Morph-KGC; October 2026) materialises: it generates RDF from the whole source in a separate step. None rewrites a SPARQL query against the source per request. Calling one from inside SPieGeL while a request is handled would mean materialising on every request, or building a cache that is in effect a store.
  • Translation per request (a virtual knowledge graph) exists mainly for relational databases with R2RML. Ontop (Java, Apache 2.0) rewrites each SPARQL query into SQL against the database, so the data is always current. It supports PostgreSQL and Trino, among others, and exposes its own SPARQL endpoint.

Because Ontop speaks SPARQL, SPieGeL's existing data source port (FR-DS-01) can reach it without a new adapter. Ontop can also be embedded as a Java library, but it is built on RDF4J, while SPieGeL's core and adapters use Jena (ADR 0004, open question 14).

Other forces:

  • Access levels rest on separate store accounts per level (FR-AC-03, NFR-SEC-02). A relational source has its own accounts, views and, in PostgreSQL, row-level security.
  • /sparql is a guarded pass-through to a store, not domain logic. The request flow sends it to "the tenant's data source", which becomes ambiguous once a tenant has several.
  • Whether the loading chain is in scope is still open question 15.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Relational sources that must be current are translated per request by Ontop, with R2RML mappings. Ontop runs as a separate service with its own SPARQL endpoint. SPieGeL configures it as a named data source (FR-DS-01) and reads it through its SPARQL adapter, like a triple store. Ontop is not embedded in SPieGeL.
  2. RML is used for materialisation only, in the loading chain. CSV, JSON, XML and Web API sources, and relational sources that may be loaded periodically, are converted by an RML processor into RDF that is loaded into a triple store. SPieGeL never runs an RML processor.
  3. There is no spiegel-adapter-rml module. Non-RDF sources need no adapter of their own in SPieGeL. This reverses the renaming amended into ADR 0004 on 2026-10-05.
  4. Access levels for an Ontop source follow the same rule as for a store: one named data source per level, each with its own database account. That account can only read what the level may see, for example through views or row-level security.
  5. Each tenant names one data source for /sparql, by default its triple store. A tenant whose data is only relational can name its Ontop source. SPieGeL does not federate queries over several sources.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The core and the data source port do not change. A relational source is a configuration matter: an Ontop service, a mapping and a named data source.
  • SPieGeL keeps one RDF library (Jena). Ontop's RDF4J dependency stays inside the Ontop service.
  • Data from a translated source is always current. In exchange, every SPieGeL query becomes SQL against the source database. The bounded pool and timeout per data source (NFR-OPS-02) protect the database, and the cache (NFR-OPS-03) limits repeated queries.
  • Running Ontop is an extra service per relational source, or per access level of one. It has to be deployed, monitored and kept up to date.
  • SPieGeL's queries (FR-RA-02) must stay within the SPARQL that Ontop supports. A prototype must confirm, before a tenant depends on it, how far Ontop supports named graphs (from rr:graphMap), property paths for hierarchies (FR-HTML-05) and DESCRIBE. Where it does not, the tenant materialises instead.
  • Keyword search (FR-SRCH-01) uses the store's full-text index. An Ontop source has none, so a tenant that needs search on relational data materialises it, or names a store for search.
  • A query on /sparql sees one source only. Combining a store with an Ontop source in one query needs SERVICE, where the store allows it, or materialisation.
  • RML mappings, processors and their schedule belong to the loading chain. Their choice depends on open question 15, not on SPieGeL.
  • Existing R2RML mappings can be used by Ontop as they are. Moving a source from translation to materialisation needs an RML processor that reads R2RML, which RMLMapper and Morph-KGC do.

docs.title: 0010. Use Jena's graph types in the core, keep SPARQL out of it
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-25

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Open question 14 asks whether the domain core uses Apache Jena's RDF types or an RDF abstraction of its own. The hexagonal design left this to an ADR. NFR-Q-01 forbids a dependency on Spring, on Jena's HTTP client and on any web framework, but not on Jena as a library.

Most of the core's work is RDF work:

  • merging the results of several queries into one description (FR-RA-01);
  • following blank nodes to a configured depth (FR-RA-04);
  • unpacking owl:unionOf and owl:intersectionOf lists (FR-RA-05);
  • adding foaf:primaryTopic and foaf:page (FR-URI-07);
  • counting triples against the ceiling (NFR-OPS-09);
  • paging large properties (FR-RA-07);
  • choosing a label by language (FR-HTML-10).

An abstraction of its own would mean writing and testing all of this again, and converting every result from and to Jena in the adapters. Its usual justification, bridging two RDF libraries, no longer applies: Ontop, which is built on RDF4J, runs as a separate service (ADR 0009). In RDF systems the graph itself is the domain model, and mapping triples into objects of our own and back adds code without adding anything.

Jena offers two levels. The graph level (org.apache.jena.graph: Graph, Node, Triple) is the foundation the rest of Jena is built on, and is small and stable. The model level (org.apache.jena.rdf.model: Model, Resource, Statement) is a richer layer on top of it.

The SPARQL engine, the HTTP client and the RIOT parsers and serialisers live in jena-arq, a separate artefact. The graph and model levels live in jena-core.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. The core uses Jena's graph level: Graph, Node and Triple from jena-core. ResourceDescription wraps a Graph. Inside a method, the core may use the model level as a view on that graph where it makes the code clearer, but its ports and domain types expose the graph level only.
  2. The core does not depend on jena-arq. It neither parses nor runs SPARQL, and does not read or write RDF formats. For the core, a query is text with bindings: a QuerySpec holds the query text, and the resource IRI is passed as a Node. Binding happens in the SPARQL adapter (NFR-SEC-04). Inspecting a query against a policy is done behind a port (ADR 0011).
  3. ArchitectureTest enforces this. Classes in the core must not depend on org.apache.jena.sparql.., org.apache.jena.query.., org.apache.jena.riot.., org.apache.jena.http.. or org.apache.jena.rdflink...

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Merging, blank nodes, lists and language tags use Jena's tested code. The adapters pass results to the core without converting them.
  • SPieGeL is tied to Jena. Replacing it would touch the core as well as the adapters. We accept this: Jena is the project's RDF library (ADR 0004), and the graph level is its most stable API.
  • spiegel-core gains a dependency on jena-core, but not on Jena's HTTP client, so NFR-Q-01 still holds.
  • Serialising RDF (Jena RIOT) happens in the adapters that render, never in the core.
  • Exposing only the graph level keeps the ports small and avoids leaking the model level's implicit state, such as prefix maps and reification, into the domain.

docs.title: 0011. Check every query against a query policy before it runs
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-25

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Two kinds of SPARQL reach a store through SPieGeL. Callers' queries arrive on /sparql (FR-SPARQL-01). Phase 2 makes that endpoint public, for every access level. Tenant queries are .rq files in the tenant configuration (FR-RA-02), written by people but loaded without review at run time.

The security boundary is the store: each access level reads through its own read-only account, which can only see that level's graphs (NFR-SEC-01, NFR-SEC-02). Checks in SPieGeL are defence in depth. Open question 29 showed that restricting graphs by rewriting queries is too weak to be the boundary, because one missed construct leaks data. Still, a query that can only do harm should be refused before it reaches the store:

  • an update (INSERT DATA, DELETE, LOAD, CLEAR, DROP);
  • a SERVICE call, which would make the store contact a host chosen by the caller, possibly an internal one (NFR-SEC-06).

A FROM, FROM NAMED or GRAPH that names a graph the level may not see is a different case. Refusing it would need a list of graphs per level in the tenant configuration, kept in step with the store by hand, and duplicating permissions that the store already enforces.

Checking query text with regular expressions is unreliable: comments, prefixes, escapes and line breaks defeat it. A parsed query can be checked reliably.

Not every store enforces graph permissions. Virtuoso does, with an account per level, and so does Fuseki with its access control; QLever and Oxigraph do not (question 29). A query on graphs, whether it names them or uses GRAPH ?g, is only safe on a store that limits what the level's account can see. A store without graph permissions is only safe if it holds nothing but what one level may see.

The core does not depend on jena-arq (ADR 0010). Adapters do not depend on each other, which ArchitectureTest enforces. A check written once must therefore be reached through a port, not shared between the web adapter and the configuration adapter.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. The core defines a QueryPolicy, as data, per tenant:

    • the allowed query forms: SELECT, CONSTRUCT, ASK and DESCRIBE;
    • SERVICE is not allowed.

    The policy names no graphs. Adding a graph to a store needs no change to the configuration. 2. The core defines an outbound port QueryInspector, which checks query text against a QueryPolicy and returns the violations, if any. spiegel-adapter-sparql implements it once: - it parses with QueryFactory using strict SPARQL 1.1 syntax (Syntax.syntaxSPARQL_11), so an update fails as a parse error; - it checks the query form; - it walks the syntax tree with an ElementWalker, and rejects every SERVICE, also when nested in a subquery, OPTIONAL or UNION; - it never matches on query text.

    Parsing knows the prefixes the tenant configures (FR-SPARQL-03). A store may predefine prefixes, such as Virtuoso's bif:; without them, queries that work on the store would fail to parse. 3. The checks run in the core, so they cannot be bypassed. RunSparqlQuery calls the inspector before every query on /sparql and refuses a violation with 400. Loading a tenant configuration calls the same inspector for every .rq file, and refuses the whole configuration if one violates the policy. The web adapter only passes the query text on. 4. The store decides which graphs a level sees. FROM, FROM NAMED and GRAPH, with an IRI or a variable, are not checked by SPieGeL: the level's account, or the store's own instance per level, only holds what the level may see. Each data source declares in the tenant configuration whether it enforces graph permissions: yes for a store with an account per level that can only read that level's graphs (Virtuoso, Fuseki with access control), no for a store without them (QLever, Oxigraph). The SPARQL adapter cannot detect this itself, so it is declared, and the adapter passes it on to the core. 5. A store without graph permissions serves one access level only. When a tenant configuration is loaded, the core refuses it if a data source that does not enforce graph permissions is shared by more than one access level. Such a store needs its own instance or index per level, as option 1 or 4 of question 29 describes. 6. Queries are never rewritten. SPieGeL refuses or passes a query; it does not add filters or VALUES to restrict graphs. 7. The SPARQL adapter enforces a timeout and a maximum number of results on every query, configured per tenant (NFR-OPS-02, NFR-PERF-03). An unbounded property path is not refused when parsing, because hierarchies need paths such as skos:broader* (FR-HTML-05). The timeout stops it. 8. The README states that each data source must be reached with a read-only account (NFR-SEC-01).

docs.title: Acceptance tests
docs.text:
The implementation includes tests with these queries and configurations. Each test names this ADR and the requirement it covers.

Input Expected INSERT DATA { … } on /sparql 400, parse error; nothing reaches the store LOAD <http://…> on /sparql 400, parse error SELECT * { SERVICE <http://internal-host/sparql> { ?s ?p ?o } } 400, SERVICE not allowed SELECT * { GRAPH <private graph> { ?s ?p ?o } } at the public level, on a store that enforces graph permissions runs; the result is empty SELECT * FROM NAMED <private graph> { GRAPH ?g { ?s ?p ?o } } at the public level, on a store that enforces graph permissions runs; the result holds no triple from a private graph SELECT * { { SELECT * { SERVICE <http://internal-host/sparql> { ?s ?p ?o } } } } (SERVICE in a subquery) 400, SERVICE not allowed SELECT * { GRAPH ?g { ?s ?p ?o } } at the public level, on a store that enforces graph permissions runs; the result holds no triple from a private graph SELECT * { ?s ?p ?o } without GRAPH or FROM, on a store whose default graph is the union of all graphs runs; the result holds no triple from a private graph SELECT * { ?s (<p>|!<p>)* ?o } (an unbounded property path) stopped at the tenant's timeout (504), within the bounded pool A query that uses a prefix the tenant configures, without declaring it parses and runs A tenant configuration with an .rq file that contains SERVICE refused when loaded A tenant configuration in which one QLever store serves two access levels refused when loaded

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One check, written once and tested once, covers both /sparql and the tenant's own queries. A faulty .rq file is found when the configuration loads, not when a visitor hits it.
  • A caller who uses SERVICE for federation is refused. Federation is left to consumers (ADR 0006, question 31).
  • The check depends on the parser. A store-specific syntax that strict SPARQL 1.1 does not accept, apart from predefined prefixes, cannot be used on /sparql.
  • Graphs need no configuration in SPieGeL. A new graph is visible to the levels whose accounts may read it, as soon as it is in the store.
  • SPieGeL offers no second check on graphs. The read-only account per level, or the separate instance per level, is the only boundary for graphs. A wrong account is not caught by SPieGeL, so the store's permissions need their own tests in the loading chain.
  • Graph permissions become an explicit, declared property of each data source. A wrong declaration is a configuration error that the loading check cannot detect.
  • Option 3 of question 29 (one store with named graphs, restricted by rewriting) is ruled out for good. Stores without graph permissions are only possible as one instance or index per level.
  • DESCRIBE is answered by the store's own algorithm, within the same account, timeout and result limit.

docs.title: 0012. Describe tenants in RDF, with one generic template and exceptions
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-25

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Almost every functional requirement depends on the tenant configuration: host names and data sources (FR-MT-01, FR-DS-01), URI templates (FR-URI-01), the queries that describe a resource (FR-RA-01 to 03), paging (FR-RA-07), layout (FR-HTML-03), labels and languages (FR-HTML-10 to 12), the licence (FR-META-02) and example queries (FR-SPARQL-04). Three open questions were still undecided:

  • question 20: the format, and whether to adopt the Linked Data API vocabulary;
  • question 19: hand-written queries, generated queries, or both;
  • question 11: where the list of valid concepts per domain comes from.

The configuration is written and maintained by the Linked Data team, who use Turtle, SHACL and SPARQL every day and also maintain each domain's vocabulary projects. Part of the configuration is RDF by nature: example queries are sh:SPARQLExecutables (FR-SPARQL-04), profiles are prof:Profiles (FR-CN-03), and the dataset description is DCAT and VoID (FR-META-01).

The Linked Data API vocabulary, as used by ELDA, covers URI templates, item templates and views, but has no profiles in the sense of Content Negotiation by Profile, no access levels, no tenants selected by host name, and no query files. Its specification has not changed since 2013. Adopting it would mean extending it in most places.

Some queries cannot be left to the tenant. Every resource needs a readable page without configuration (FR-HTML-01), so a generic description query must exist. Each large property is queried with LIMIT N+1 (FR-RA-07), and front-page blocks and labels have defaults (FR-HTML-09, FR-HTML-10). The core cannot build SPARQL syntax trees (ADR 0010).

The predecessor compiles a list of valid concepts per domain into its routes. Every new concept therefore needs a change to the configuration, and the lists differ per environment.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. The tenant configuration is Turtle, in a small vocabulary of SPieGeL's own. It reuses existing terms wherever they fit: prof: for profiles, sh: for example queries, prefixes and patterns, dcat:, dct: and void: for the dataset description, and the Linked Data API's api:uriTemplate and api:itemTemplate. The proposed namespace is https://w3id.org/spiegel/config#, a neutral, persistent IRI, so that organisations other than the department can use it.
  2. SPieGeL validates the configuration when it loads it, with SHACL shapes that it ships, and checks every query file against the query policy (ADR 0011). One violation refuses the whole configuration.
  3. The core never sees Turtle. The configuration adapter turns it into the core's types: Tenant, DataSource, UriTemplate, ResourceType, QuerySpec and Profile.
  4. No secrets in the configuration. A data source names its credentials by a key; their values come from the platform's secret store (ADR 0013).
  5. One generic template covers every concept. A tenant normally declares one ResourceType with /id/{concept}/{id} and /doc/{concept}/{id}. Without anything else, it uses SPieGeL's default queries. A new concept in the data works at once, with no change to the configuration.
  6. Exceptions are optional and describe only what differs. A more specific template, such as /doc/emissie/{id}, adds its own queries, profiles or layout and inherits everything else. The most specific template wins (step 4 of the request flow). An exception is chosen by path, which is known before any query runs. Choosing by rdf:type may be added later, first for the HTML layout (FR-HTML-06), where the type is known after the queries anyway.

  7. Queries are default templates plus hand-written files. SPieGeL ships .rq templates for:

    • the generic description, bounded to its subject (FR-RA-06);
    • labels (FR-HTML-10);
    • one page of a large property (FR-RA-07);
    • the default front-page blocks (FR-HTML-09).

    The templates take bindings such as ?resource, ?property and ?lang. A limit is an attribute of the QuerySpec, applied by the SPARQL adapter. A tenant replaces a default or adds to it with its own .rq files. Generating queries from SHACL shapes (as Prez does) may come later, as an adapter that supplies QuerySpecs; it is not built now. 8. Large properties are declared once, for all tenants in the shared defaults or per tenant, such as dct:hasPart or skos:member with a page size. A specific template may override this. 9. Template variables are typed by a pattern, and the data decides whether a resource exists. A variable has an sh:pattern; a value that does not match gives 404 without a query. A value that matches is looked up, and an empty description gives 404 (or 301 or 410, FR-URI-08 to 11). A negative result is cached per data version (NFR-OPS-03). A tenant that wants a closed list writes it as a pattern, such as ^(dossier|besluit)$.

A sketch of a tenant:

<#imjv> a spiegel:Tenant ;
    spiegel:hostName "data.imjv.omgeving.vlaanderen.be" ;
    dct:license <https://data.vlaanderen.be/id/licentie/modellicentie-gratis-hergebruik/v1.0> ;
    spiegel:languagePriority ( "nl" "en" "" ) ;
    spiegel:dataSource <#store-public> ;
    spiegel:sparqlDataSource <#store-public> ;
    spiegel:resourceType <#generic>, <#emissie> .

<#store-public> a spiegel:DataSource ;
    spiegel:accessLevel spiegel:Public ;
    spiegel:credentialKey "imjv-public" ;
    spiegel:enforcesGraphPermissions true .

<#generic> a spiegel:ResourceType ;
    api:itemTemplate "/id/{concept}/{id}" ;
    api:uriTemplate  "/doc/{concept}/{id}" .

# An exception: only what differs from the generic template.
<#emissie> a spiegel:ResourceType ;
    api:uriTemplate "/doc/emissie/{id}" ;
    spiegel:query [ spiegel:file "queries/emissie-full.rq" ; spiegel:profile <#full> ] .

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The configuration is written in the language its authors already use, and validated with SHACL, which they know. Profiles, example queries and the dataset description can be published as they are.
  • A typical tenant is small: a host name, data sources, a licence, a language order, one generic template and a few exceptions. Adding a concept to the data needs no configuration.
  • SPieGeL owns a vocabulary and its SHACL shapes, which must be documented, versioned and kept backwards compatible for existing tenants.
  • Every request for a path that matches a pattern but does not exist costs one bounded query, until its negative result is cached. The rate limit (NFR-OPS-08) and the bounded pool (NFR-OPS-02) limit the cost.
  • People outside the Linked Data team, for example operations, do not edit this configuration. What they manage (credentials, pool sizes, timeouts per environment) stays in the application's Spring configuration.
  • The namespace must be registered at w3id.org before the first release that reads it. Until then the vocabulary may still change.
  • Question 18 stays as decided in FR-URI-11: a move or removal of a single URI is data in the store, a move of a whole pattern or host name is a rewrite rule in this configuration.

docs.title: 0013. Deliver tenant configuration as a versioned artefact
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-25

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Open question 16 asks how the configuration reaches a running SPieGeL in production. The tenant configuration is Turtle with .rq files (ADR 0012). The requirements constrain the answer:

  • NFR-OPS-06: configuration is external to the build artefact and under version control;
  • NFR-OPS-07: a deployment never mixes incompatible versions behind one host name;
  • ADR 0011: a configuration that fails validation is refused;
  • FR-SPARQL-04: every example query is run against the domain's store, so that one that no longer works is noticed.

The options were:

  • a versioned artefact, mounted read-only and rolled out with a rolling restart;
  • files synchronised live from Git on every node, reloaded without a restart;
  • a configuration server, such as Spring Cloud Config, with a refresh.

The last two make a change visible in seconds, but nodes run different versions until all of them have synchronised, and a configuration server is one more service to run. Most domains change their configuration rarely: their data changes far more often than their structure (see Performance and availability).

The configuration must also live somewhere. Each domain already has vocabulary projects under version control, but keeping the configuration there would make one rollout depend on many repositories.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. One central configuration repository, with a directory per tenant and a directory for shared defaults, such as the large properties and label sources that hold for every tenant.
  2. CI validates every change before anything is built:
    • the SHACL shapes of the configuration vocabulary;
    • the query policy, for every .rq file;
    • every example query, run against the domain's store (FR-SPARQL-04).
  3. CI builds a versioned artefact from the repository and publishes it to the departmental Artifactory.
  4. In production the artefact is mounted read-only and rolled out with a rolling restart. SPieGeL does not reload configuration at run time in production. A configuration that fails to load stops the new node from starting, and the nodes on the previous version keep serving. During development, SPieGeL may reload a local directory on change.
  5. The configuration version is visible: in the logs at start-up and in the health endpoint (NFR-OPS-04), so that every response can be traced to a configuration.
  6. Credentials come from the platform's secret store, looked up by the key that the configuration names. They are never in the repository or the artefact.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One version of the configuration runs behind a host name at a time, and a faulty configuration never replaces a working one.
  • A change takes minutes (build, publish, roll out), not seconds. That suits domains whose configuration changes rarely. Urgent changes to a single URI, such as a removal under the GDPR, do not wait for it, because they are data in the store (FR-URI-10, FR-URI-11).
  • The Linked Data team works in one repository for all tenants. Changes to a domain's vocabulary and to its configuration are made in separate repositories, so a change that needs both needs two merges.
  • CI needs read access to each domain's store, at the public level, to run the example queries.
  • The configuration repository is separate from SPieGeL's own public repository. Whether it can be public too depends on what it contains: it holds host names and query files, but no credentials.

docs.title: 0014. Keep Linked-Data-specific components in SPieGeL, contribute generic ones to Flux
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-25

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
SPieGeL's HTML follows the Flux design system (ADR 0005). The analysis listed seven components that Flux does not offer as such: a resource description, an RDF term, incoming relations, a hierarchy tree, a collection table, a geometry map and a SPARQL editor (see Design system: Flux). Open question 23 asked whether they live in SPieGeL or in Flux.

The Flux team reviewed the seven against Flux 2.21.0 in a working document of 16 October 2026. It sorted them into three kinds:

  • composition: markup in the server templates, built entirely from Flux components, with no custom element of its own (resource description, RDF term);
  • thin layer: a small component that loads data and passes it to an existing Flux component, which provides the look (incoming relations, hierarchy tree, collection table, geometry map);
  • new: no Flux base, so a new interface that follows Flux's conventions and CSS variables (SPARQL editor).

For the hierarchy tree, Flux 2.21.0 offers vl-cascader, a drilldown with a breadcrumb that loads each level on demand. The analysis had found no base for it. Whether a drilldown is enough, or whether data structures need another kind of visualisation, has been put back to the Flux team as a broader question (open question 39).

Flux accepts contributions from other teams, provided they are backwards compatible and the approach is agreed with the Flux team first. A contribution makes a component reusable, but ties its release to Flux's.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. What is specific to Linked Data stays in SPieGeL. What turns out to be generic is offered to Flux, backwards compatible and agreed with the Flux team beforehand.

  2. Per component:

    Component Kind Where Resource description composition server template in SPieGeL RDF term composition server template in SPieGeL; the choice of label and language is made on the server Incoming relations thin layer on vl-accordion, vl-pager, vl-loader component in SPieGeL Hierarchy thin layer, candidate vl-cascader adapter in SPieGeL; the visualisation itself waits for open question 39. A generic tree or structure view would be a Flux component Collection table thin layer on vl-rich-data-table, vl-search-filter, vl-pager controller in SPieGeL; the pattern for paging on the server may be offered to Flux Geometry map thin layer on vl-map, vl-map-features-layer component in SPieGeL; WKT as an input format for the features layer may be offered to Flux SPARQL editor new component in SPieGeL, wrapping an existing editor (open question 37)

  3. SPieGeL's own components follow Flux's conventions:

    • Lit elements with their own prefix, not vl-;
    • Flux's CSS variables, with no inline styles or scripts (NFR-UI-03);
    • Cypress component tests with cypress-axe (NFR-UI-02).
  4. Content stays on the server. Compositions are written into the page by the templates, in the light DOM or in slots, so that the page is readable without JavaScript (NFR-UI-04). Thin layers only load more data and add interaction.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• SPieGeL builds three to four small components and one wrapper, not seven components. Five of the seven add no new visual element to the house style.
  • The templates carry more of the work: the resource description and the RDF term are markup patterns, tested on the server side (NFR-Q-02), not custom elements.
  • Contributions to Flux, such as paging on the server or WKT input, need agreement and follow Flux's release cycle. Until they are released, SPieGeL keeps its own version.
  • The hierarchy on subject pages of concept schemes, concepts, catalogues and datasets (FR-HTML-05) cannot be finished before open question 39 is answered.
  • Open points that Flux has to answer, such as a lazy-loading event on vl-accordion or a vl-pager without a total, are listed in Design system: Flux. SPieGeL works around a missing feature until Flux offers it.
  • The licence of Flux and access to its packages for external contributors (open question 22) are not settled by this decision.

docs.title: 0015. Serve large and follow-up data as paged Hydra lists
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-25

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Two open questions meet here:

  • Open question 24: do the interactive components query /sparql from the browser, as the predecessor's do, or call endpoints on the server?
  • Open question 35: which vocabulary describes the pages of a large property (FR-RA-07)?

FR-RA-07 already requires that a large property has a paged list with its own URI, and that HTML exploration (FR-HTML-05) uses the same pages, so that HTML and RDF follow one rule. The thin-layer components of ADR 0014 need exactly such lists:

  • the collection table pages through the members of a collection, catalogue or organisation;
  • incoming relations show the resources that refer to the subject, per predicate, with a count, and page through them. They are not part of the description (ADR 0006), so FR-RA-07 did not cover them;
  • the hierarchy (candidate vl-cascader, open question 39) loads the children of one node at a time, such as skos:narrower or dcat:dataset.

Queries built in the browser live outside the tenant configuration, cannot be cached per access level, and expose store dialects to the client. A separate JSON API per component would keep queries on the server, but adds a contract next to the RDF that only SPieGeL's own components can use.

The Flux team asked whether vl-pager can work without total-items, because SPieGeL asks for N+1 rows instead of counting. A COUNT on a large store is costly. Yet the mock-up of the incoming relations block shows a count per relation.

The Hydra vocabulary describes a page as a hydra:PartialCollectionView of a hydra:Collection, with hydra:first, hydra:previous and hydra:next, and an optional hydra:totalItems. TREE is the basis of event streams, and is made to fragment a collection by a value, such as time.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Follow-up data are paged lists, served as Linked Data. The interactive components do not query /sparql, and SPieGeL offers no separate JSON API. A component requests the URI of a list as JSON-LD; a harvester can request the same list as Turtle.
  2. Lists use Hydra. A list is a hydra:Collection whose members are hydra:member. A page is a hydra:PartialCollectionView with hydra:first, hydra:previous and hydra:next. The last page has no hydra:next. A component therefore knows from hydra:next whether there is another page, without a total. TREE remains the vocabulary of event streams.

  3. A list's URI is its subject's doc URI with reserved query parameters, in the style of _format and _profile (FR-CN-02, FR-CN-03):

    Kind of list URI Values of a property of the subject /doc/collectie/dossier?_property=co:element Resources that refer to the subject through one predicate /doc/stof/benzeen?_inverse=imjv:stof Overview of incoming predicates, with a count each /doc/stof/benzeen?_inverse A further page …&_page=2

    Properties are prefixed names, with the prefixes the tenant configures (FR-SPARQL-03). No path segment is reserved, so lists cannot collide with URI templates, including hierarchical ones such as ELI. 4. Which lists exist. _property is answered for properties declared as large (ADR 0012) and for the properties the components need, such as skos:hasTopConcept, skos:narrower, dcat:dataset and dcat:catalog, in the shared defaults. Other properties are part of the description and get 404 as a list. _inverse is answered for any predicate, because incoming relations are generic. 5. A description links to its lists. It holds the first N values of a large property and a hydra:view to the list (FR-RA-07). 6. Each member comes with its label, chosen by the tenant's language priority (FR-HTML-10), so that a table, a pager or a tree can show it without another request. 7. Pages have a fixed size and a stable order. The default size is 100, configurable per tenant and per property, with a maximum. Members are ordered by their IRI, so _page=N gives the same members within one data version. Each page is queried with LIMIT N+1 and an offset, within the same timeout and ceiling as any query (NFR-OPS-02, NFR-OPS-09). 8. Counts are bounded and cached. A count runs up to a ceiling, for example 1,000, and is shown as "more than 1,000" above it. It is cached per data version (NFR-OPS-03). In RDF, hydra:totalItems is given only when the count is exact. 9. Lists follow the same flow as descriptions: tenant, access level, cache under the data version with the access level in the key, and bounded queries (NFR-SEC-03). Their queries are SPieGeL's default templates or a tenant's own QuerySpecs (ADR 0012). 10. JSON-LD for lists uses a fixed @context, published by SPieGeL, so that a component reads plain JSON keys such as member, next and label instead of expanded IRIs.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One mechanism serves the collection table, incoming relations, the hierarchy and harvesters. Its queries are configurable, cached and authorised like descriptions. No query is built in the browser.
  • The answer to the Flux team: vl-pager needs no total. "Next" depends on hydra:next, and a count, when there is one, is bounded.
  • Incoming relations become reachable for RDF clients without SPARQL, while staying out of the description itself, as ADR 0006 requires.
  • Ordering and offsets cost more on deep pages of very large lists, because the store sorts before it skips. Caching per data version softens this. If it proves too slow, a cursor that continues after the last member can replace _page without changing the URIs that clients follow: they only follow hydra:next.
  • _inverse for any predicate lets callers request costly lists. The timeout, the bounded pool and the rate limit (NFR-OPS-08) limit the damage.
  • The fixed @context covers lists only. A @context for descriptions in general is a separate requirement that is still missing.
  • Hydra is a Community Group draft that hardly moves. SPieGeL uses only its stable core terms.

docs.title: 0016. Answer errors to machines with problem details (RFC 9457)
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-25
  • Amended: 2026-10-26: added method-not-allowed, internal-error, and the 406 for a description that cannot be written in the format asked for (spec 001)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The request flow lists SPieGeL's errors (E1 to E7) and how HTML shows them (vl-http-error-message), but not what a client gets that asked for Turtle, JSON-LD or SPARQL results. Some rules already hold:

  • an unknown resource and one the caller may not see give the same 404 (FR-URI-06, NFR-SEC-07);
  • a 502 or 504 never includes the store's error message or the query text (E2, E3);
  • 429 and 503 carry Retry-After (NFR-OPS-02, NFR-OPS-08);
  • a 410 is not an error but a tombstone, described in RDF (FR-URI-10).

On /sparql, a 400 is most useful when it says where the query went wrong, or which rule of the query policy it broke (ADR 0011).

RFC 9457 (Problem Details for HTTP APIs) defines application/problem+json, with a type IRI per kind of problem, a title, the status, a detail and an instance. HTTP libraries in most languages understand it. An error could also be negotiated into the requested RDF format, with Hydra's error terms, but an error is not data about the resource, and a client checks the status before it reads the body. For a 406, SPieGeL cannot answer in a requested format by definition.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. A browser gets an HTML error page; every other client gets application/problem+json, whatever RDF format or result format it asked for, including on 406. HTML is chosen by the same negotiation as for descriptions (FR-CN-08).

  2. Every problem has a stable type IRI, under https://w3id.org/spiegel/problem/, documented with SPieGeL. For example:

    Status type When 400 …/problem/invalid-query /sparql: a syntax error, an update, or a query that breaks the query policy 400 …/problem/invalid-request an invalid parameter, such as _page or _property 404 …/problem/not-found no template, no resource, or a resource the caller may not see 405 …/problem/method-not-allowed a method other than those the resource allows, with Allow 406 …/problem/not-acceptable no acceptable media type, or the description cannot be written in the format asked for 429 …/problem/rate-limited this client is over its limit 500 …/problem/internal-error an unexpected failure inside SPieGeL itself 502 …/problem/source-error a data source failed 503 …/problem/overloaded the pool or queue of a data source is full 504 …/problem/source-timeout a data source did not answer in time

  3. The body is safe by construction. title and detail are written by SPieGeL, in English, and never copy a store's message, a stack trace or a query text. An internal-error has a generic title and no detail; the cause is in the logs, under the request identifier. The 404 body is the same for a resource that does not exist and for one the caller may not see.

  4. instance carries the request identifier as a urn:uuid: URI, the same identifier that the logs use (NFR-OPS-05), so that a report can be traced without exposing anything else.
  5. A query error on /sparql says where. An invalid-query problem adds line and column from the parser, or the policy rule that was broken, such as "SERVICE is not allowed". It does not echo the query.
  6. Error responses keep the response rules: CORS as for any public response (NFR-OPEN-01), so that scripts in a browser can read the error; Retry-After on 429 and 503; Vary where the format was negotiated; and Cache-Control: no-store on 429 and every 5xx.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Clients get one predictable error format, which HTTP libraries already parse, for descriptions, lists, /sparql and the dataset description alike.
  • The type IRIs become part of SPieGeL's public contract: new ones may be added, existing ones keep their meaning. The namespace must be registered at w3id.org, like the configuration vocabulary (ADR 0012).
  • An RDF client gets JSON on an error, not RDF. We accept this: an error is not a description of the resource.
  • A tombstone (410) and a moved resource (301) stay outside this scheme, because they are answers about the resource, not errors.
  • The error texts for machines are English only. HTML error pages follow the visitor's language (FR-HTML-12).

docs.title: 0017. Serve framed JSON-LD with a generated, frozen context
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-25

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
FR-CN-01 makes every description available as JSON-LD, but says nothing about its shape. Written without a frame and without a context, JSON-LD is a flat @graph of nodes with full IRIs as keys and every value in an array. A web developer must then find the subject among the nodes, look up blank nodes by their identifier and join labels of linked resources by hand. ELDA and Prez offer short names instead (see the landscape).

Two different things are needed:

  • a frame, which decides the shape: a tree with the subject at its root, with nested values;
  • a context, which decides the keys and values: prefLabel instead of an IRI, an IRI value as "@id", a language map instead of a list of tagged strings, always an array or a single value.

The frame can be the same for every description, because a description is bounded to its subject (ADR 0006): its own properties, nested blank nodes, and the label and type of linked resources.

A context can be derived by an algorithm. Per predicate it chooses a short name, and finds whether values are IRIs, which datatype literals have, whether there are languages and whether there can be several values. SHACL shapes say this directly (sh:path, sh:nodeKind, sh:class, sh:datatype, sh:maxCount). Where a domain has no shapes, the derived structure of its data says it (FR-HTML-15).

Deriving a context at run time, per response or per data version, makes keys and shapes depend on the data. A second value turns a string into an array, and a new predicate in another namespace can take the name title. Client code then breaks silently, although the RDF is correct. A key that a client relies on must keep its meaning and its shape.

The JSON-LD 1.1 processor in Jena 6 is Titanium, which supports compaction and framing. Whether Jena's writer passes a frame through, or SPieGeL calls Titanium directly, is still to be checked.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Every JSON-LD description is framed by one generic frame:

    • the subject, the id URI of the request, is the root object;
    • blank nodes are nested in place (FR-RA-04);
    • linked resources appear as an object with only what the description holds about them: id, label and type;
    • @embed is @always, so that a node has the same shape wherever it appears.

    The frame needs no configuration. 2. Each tenant has a context, generated and then frozen. A generator, shipped with SPieGeL as a tool, proposes the context in the CI of the configuration repository (ADR 0013): - from the domain's SHACL shapes first, and otherwise from the derived structure of its data; - names: the local name of each predicate. On a collision, the predicate in the namespace that comes first in the tenant's prefix order keeps the short name, and the other one gets a prefixed name; - values: "@type": "@id" for IRIs, the datatype for typed literals, "@container": "@language" for language-tagged text, and "@container": "@set" unless the shape says there is at most one value; - id and type as aliases of @id and @type.

    The Linked Data team reviews the proposal. The result is a file in the configuration, like any other. 3. A published context only grows. A term, once published, keeps its IRI, its type and its container. New terms may be added. A change to an existing term needs a new context version with its own URI, and the earlier versions remain served. 4. SPieGeL serves the contexts itself, from the tenant's own host, under a versioned URI such as /context/v3.jsonld, with long-lived caching. A description refers to it by URI. No context is fetched from another host at run time (NFR-SEC-06). 5. What the context does not know stays lossless. A predicate without a term becomes a prefixed name, or a full IRI, so that an RDF client always gets the same triples. 6. Plain JSON is offered as well. A request for application/json gets the same framed document, with the context in a Link header (rel="http://www.w3.org/ns/json-ld#context"), as JSON-LD 1.1 allows. 7. The paged lists of ADR 0015 use the same mechanism, with the Hydra terms they need added to the context.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A web developer gets a document such as data.prefLabel.nl or data.broader[0].prefLabel.nl, and it is still valid JSON-LD.
  • The context is a public contract per tenant. Reviewing additions is a small, recurring task for the Linked Data team, and it is where a client-breaking change would be noticed.
  • New predicates in the data appear as prefixed names until the context is extended. Nothing breaks, but the JSON is less tidy until then.
  • Domains with SHACL shapes get the best contexts. Without shapes, the generator guesses from the data, for example "at most one value" where every resource happens to have one, so its proposals need more care in review.
  • A short spike must confirm how framing and compaction are done with Jena 6 and Titanium, and what they cost per response against NFR-PERF-01.
  • The context path, such as /context/, is reserved on every host, like /sparql.

docs.title: 0018. Minimise personal data from requests; leave personal data in the data to the store
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-25

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Personal data reaches SPieGeL in two ways.

In the published data. Some domains hold personal data, such as the names of people behind a company. Whether it may be published, and at which access level, is decided by the data owner. The store and the loading chain keep personal data in separate graphs that only the accounts of the levels allowed to see them can read (NFR-SEC-02, ADR 0011). A public export starts from an allowlist of graphs (open question 29). SPieGeL relies on this; it does not decide what is personal.

In the requests. Every request carries data that never passes through a graph:

  • the visitor's IP address, which the Court of Justice of the EU treats as personal data (Breyer, C-582/14, 2016);
  • what a visitor types: a search term (FR-SRCH-01) or a SPARQL query (FR-SPARQL-01), which may contain a name;
  • from phase 2, the identity of an authenticated caller (FR-AC-01).

These end up only in SPieGeL's own logs, metrics and rate-limit counters (NFR-OPS-05, NFR-OPS-08). There, SPieGeL is responsible.

Logs serve real needs: tracing an error, finding slow queries, investigating abuse. They do not need the visitor's full address, what they searched for, or who they are by name. A plain hash of a short query that contains a name can be reversed by trying candidate names, so it is not enough to hide it.

Responses with personal data reach callers at higher access levels. SPieGeL caches them under the access level (NFR-SEC-03), marks them private, and invalidates them with the data version (NFR-OPS-03). Public responses may be kept by shared caches outside SPieGeL, such as proxies, which matters when something was published in error and is removed (FR-URI-10).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Personal data in the published data is the store's responsibility. SPieGeL serves it only through the account of a level that may read it, and adds no other protection of its own. Data owners, the loading chain and the store keep it in separate, non-public graphs.
  2. SPieGeL minimises personal data from requests in its logs:
    • IP addresses are truncated: IPv4 to /24, IPv6 to /48;
    • an authenticated caller is logged as a keyed hash (HMAC) of the token's subject, never by name or e-mail address;
    • a URL is logged as its path, the names of its query parameters, and only the values of _format, _profile, _page, _property and _inverse;
    • search terms and the text of SPARQL queries are not logged. A query on /sparql is logged as a keyed hash, with its duration, status and number of results, so that a recurring slow query can be recognised without its text;
    • the key of the hashes is a secret that changes at least as often as logs are deleted, so that old hashes cannot be linked to new ones.
  3. Rate-limit counters may use the full IP address, because they must tell clients apart. They live only in memory or in the shared counter, with a lifetime of minutes, and are never written to a log.
  4. Metrics carry no personal data: they are labelled by tenant, data source, resource type, status and media type, never by IRI, IP address or caller.
  5. How long logs are kept is configuration. The value is set by the organisation that runs SPieGeL, with its data protection officer. SPieGeL ships a short default.
  6. Caching follows the access level. A response at a non-public level is Cache-Control: private and is cached by SPieGeL only under its access level and data version. A public response may be kept by shared caches for a short time only, minutes by default and configurable per tenant, and is then revalidated with its ETag.
  7. No personal data in configuration or tests. Example queries, tenant configuration and test fixtures use invented or public data, never real personal data. Reviews of the configuration repository check this (ADR 0013).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A log line is enough to trace an error through the request identifier (ADR 0016), and to find slow or abusive patterns, but not to see who searched for whom.
  • Investigating abuse from one address works through the rate limiter and the reverse proxy, not through SPieGeL's logs. The reverse proxy's own access log, with full addresses, is outside this decision; the organisation that runs it sets its own retention.
  • A slow query can be recognised by its hash, but not read. To analyse it, someone must reproduce it, for example from the client who reported it.
  • Short public caching means more revalidation requests. They are cheap, because a 304 from the data version needs no query (NFR-OPS-03), but shared caches help less than with a long lifetime.
  • Removing personal data that was published in error is done in the store and the loading chain. SPieGeL's cache follows with the next data version, and shared caches within minutes.
  • The secret for the hashes is one more secret to manage, from the platform's secret store, like the store credentials.

docs.title: 0019. Advertise entry points to search engines, with schema.org for datasets and terms
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-25

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Three kinds of finder look for what SPieGeL publishes, and each reads something different:

  • search engines read robots.txt, sitemaps, the HTML and schema.org in JSON-LD;
  • dataset search services, such as Google Dataset Search, data.europa.eu and the Flemish open data catalogue, harvest DCAT or read schema.org Dataset. SPieGeL already describes each domain in DCAT and VoID (FR-META-01);
  • link previews, in chat tools and social media, read Open Graph tags. Subject pages are the landing pages for links from elsewhere (ADR 0007), so a shared URI should preview well.

Machines already find the other formats of a page: the HTML has <link rel="alternate"> to its RDF formats (FR-HTML-04), and every response has Link headers with rel="alternate" per format and profile (FR-CN-04). A thing's other distributions, such as its feature in OGC API Features, appear only as visible links (FR-HTML-13, ADR 0007).

The HTML also embeds the domain's own description as JSON-LD (FR-HTML-04). Search engines ignore terms they do not know; they understand schema.org. The DCAT 3 specification includes a mapping from DCAT to schema.org. SKOS concepts and schemes correspond to schema:DefinedTerm and schema:DefinedTermSet.

Advertising every resource has a cost. The predecessor's logs already show many crawlers, each fetching different resources in every format (Performance and availability). A sitemap of every subject would mean listing all subjects for each data version, and would draw more crawling to pages, such as a single measurement, that search engines often do not index anyway. Variants of one page, such as ?_format=ttl, ?lang=en, or the paged lists of ADR 0015, would be indexed as duplicates.

Search engines index reliably what is in the HTML as it is sent. This depends on rendering on the server (open question 40).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. A sitemap lists the entry points, not every resource. /sitemap.xml on each tenant's host lists the doc URIs of the front page, catalogues and datasets, concept schemes, collections and vocabulary (ns) pages. Which resource types are entry points is configurable per tenant (ADR 0012); the shared defaults name dcat:Catalog, dcat:Dataset, skos:ConceptScheme, co:Collection and owl:Ontology. The sitemap is built with bounded queries, like a front-page block, and cached per data version. It is split into files of at most 50,000 URLs, with a sitemap index when needed, and carries the data version's release date as lastmod. Other pages remain reachable by following links.
  2. robots.txt per tenant names the sitemap and excludes /sparql and the paged lists (?_property, ?_inverse, ?_page). It never excludes the format variants (.ttl, ?_format=…), so that Linked Data crawlers can follow the alternates. A tenant can extend it. Outside production, robots.txt excludes everything by default, so that test environments are not indexed.
  3. Each page names its canonical URL: <link rel="canonical"> points to the doc URI without format, language or paging parameters. Canonical and alternates complement each other: the canonical names the page, the alternates name the same content in other formats.
  4. Alternates also point to the thing's other distributions. Where a link of FR-HTML-13 has a media type, such as application/geo+json for a feature in OGC API Features, it is also given as <link rel="alternate" type="…"> in the HTML and as a Link header on every format. Every page also links to its domain's dataset description with rel="describedby" (FR-META-01). Machines can then follow a thing from SPieGeL to its other forms, as ADR 0007 intends for people.
  5. Responses to authenticated callers are not indexed: they carry X-Robots-Tag: noindex.
  6. SPieGeL adds schema.org in a separate JSON-LD block, next to the domain's own description, which stays unchanged (FR-HTML-04). The translation is a fixed table in SPieGeL, not configuration:
    • dcat:Dataset and dcat:Catalog become schema:Dataset and schema:DataCatalog, following the DCAT 3 mapping: name, description, licence, publisher, keywords, distributions;
    • skos:Concept and skos:ConceptScheme become schema:DefinedTerm and schema:DefinedTermSet;
    • every other page gets name, description, url and identifier (its id URI).
  7. Every page has Open Graph tags: og:title (the label), og:description, og:url (the canonical URL) and og:type.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Datasets and code lists, the pages people actually search for, can be found in search engines and in Google Dataset Search, without configuration per tenant.
  • Crawling is not invited to every measurement or emission record, which keeps load in proportion. Those pages can still be found through links and through the dataset descriptions.
  • The schema.org block is a lossy summary for search engines. The domain's own JSON-LD, the RDF formats and the dataset description stay the full sources.
  • The translation table is SPieGeL's responsibility: when schema.org or the DCAT mapping changes, SPieGeL follows.
  • Server-side rendering becomes one more criterion for open question 40: a page built in the browser is indexed later and less reliably.
  • Test environments with production IRIs are kept out of search engines by default; a tenant that wants otherwise must say so explicitly.
  • A thing's other distributions become discoverable by machines, not only by people. The link templates of FR-HTML-13 must then say which media type each link has. A link to an event stream (open question 30) can be added the same way later.

docs.title: 0020. Key the cache by profile, and tag responses with data and configuration version
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-26

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The request flow caches the assembled ResourceDescription, an RDF graph, under (tenant, resource IRI, profile, access level) in step 10. The media type is not part of the key: a description cached for a Turtle request serves a later JSON-LD or HTML request with the same profile, and only serialisation is repeated. The chapter asks for this choice to be confirmed in an ADR.

The ETag is the tenant's data version, combined with the variant: media type, profile and language (NFR-OPS-03). A cached description stays valid until the loading chain signals a new data version.

A response, however, depends on more than the data:
