  • the tenant's configuration (ADR 0012): which queries run, how deep blank nodes go, which profiles exist, which context shapes the JSON-LD (ADR 0017), which templates, presentation rules and label sources build the HTML;
  • SPieGeL itself: its serialisers, its frame, its default templates and its schema.org table (ADR 0019).

Both change without a new data version. A configuration is rolled out as a new artefact with a rolling restart (ADR 0013). Today the cache is in memory, so a restart empties it, but a shared cache is planned (CachePort, Hexagonal design). And whatever SPieGeL's own cache does, a client or proxy that revalidates with an ETag of the data version alone gets 304 Not Modified after a rollout, and keeps the old content. For a domain loaded a few times a year, that lasts months. During a rolling restart, two nodes serve different content under the same tag.

An ETag promises that the same tag means the same representation. That holds only if the tag covers everything the representation depends on.

Serialising per response has a cost, largest for framed JSON-LD and HTML. The predecessor's logs show that the same resource is rarely asked for in several formats (Performance and availability), so a cache of serialised bytes would save little, and would itself depend on the context and templates.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. The cache holds the description, not its serialisation. The key is (tenant, resource IRI, profile, access level). The media type and the interface language are not part of it; they are applied after the cache, in step 14.
  2. A cached description is immutable. It is a read-only graph that several requests may serialise at the same time.
  3. The cache is bound to the deployment. An entry is valid for one data version, one configuration version of the tenant and one SPieGeL version. A shared cache keeps entries of different versions apart, so that nodes on the old and the new version never serve each other's descriptions during a rolling restart.
  4. The ETag covers everything a response depends on: the data version, the configuration version, the SPieGeL version and the variant (media type, profile, language). It is sent as a short hash of these parts, so that it reveals no internal versions.
  5. The ETag is weak (W/"…"). Two nodes may write the same graph in a different order of triples or prefixes; the representations are equivalent, not byte for byte identical. Weak tags suffice for If-None-Match and 304.
  6. No cache of serialised bytes, until the spike of ADR 0017 or measurements against NFR-PERF-01 show that serialisation from the cache is too slow.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One description serves every format of a profile, so its queries run once, whatever format is asked for first.
  • Turtle and HTML share an entry only when they use the same profile. Where a resource type has a lighter default profile for HTML (step 7), HTML has its own entry.
  • After a rollout of configuration or of SPieGeL, every description is fetched again once, and every client gets the new content on its next revalidation. Because configuration changes rarely, this costs little.
  • Every response from the cache is still serialised. Its cost counts towards the target for cached responses (p95 ≤ 50 ms, NFR-PERF-01), and must be measured, for JSON-LD in particular.
  • The configuration version and the SPieGeL version must be known at run time; ADR 0013 already makes the configuration version visible.
  • The 304 after step 13 needs no query and no serialisation: the tag is computed from versions and the negotiated variant alone.

docs.title: 0021. Take labels of external vocabularies from reviewed extracts in the configuration
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-26

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Every IRI on a page is shown by its label (FR-HTML-10). For terms of external vocabularies, such as dct:title, skos:broader or dcat:Dataset, FR-HTML-11 consults label sources in order: the domain's own data source, then a shared vocabulary source, then the fallback of a prefixed name or the full IRI. Which sources are the default, and what the shared source is, was open question 26. Fetching a vocabulary from the web while a request is handled is ruled out (NFR-SEC-06).

This decision covers terms of vocabularies: a few thousand properties, classes and individuals, the same for every tenant, which rarely change. It does not cover resources of other domains that the data links to, such as a concept from a code list of another tenant. Those change with that tenant's data and have their own access levels; they are open question 42.

Loading every external ontology into every store means maintaining the same ontologies many times, in the loading chain. Prez bundles labels of common vocabularies with the server instead (Prez code review).

The RDF and SPARQL plugin for IntelliJ IDEA solves the same problem for an editor. It downloads each vocabulary ahead of time, from a download URL that is the namespace IRI by default but can be overridden, and keeps a snapshot in RDF Thrift with the date of the download. It refreshes only on request. For its hover texts and completion it does not use the graph, but an index that holds per term its kind (class or property), its label (rdfs:label, skos:prefLabel, dct:title) and its description (rdfs:comment, skos:definition, dct:description), each with its language. Two observations from its settings:

  • a namespace IRI is not always a usable source: XSD and schema.org are downloaded from a repository instead;
  • whole vocabularies can be large: QUDT's units are 81,000 triples, mostly labels in many languages.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Labels of external terms come from, in order: the domain's own data source, through the label query of the HTML profile (request flow); the tenant's own vocabulary extracts; the shared vocabulary extracts; then the fallback of FR-HTML-10.
  2. The shared source is part of the configuration, not a store. The shared defaults of the configuration repository (ADR 0013) hold a list of vocabularies and an extract per vocabulary. A tenant can add vocabularies of its own in the same way.
  3. Each vocabulary in the list has a namespace and a download URL, which is the namespace IRI unless it is overridden, as for XSD and schema.org.

  4. An extract holds only what pages need. That is, per term in the namespace:

    • its kind: class, property or other;
    • its labels (rdfs:label, skos:prefLabel, dct:title);
    • its descriptions (rdfs:comment, skos:definition, dct:description).

    Only the interface languages of SPieGeL (open question 27) and literals without a language tag are kept. The extract is sorted Turtle, so that its diffs can be read, and records its source URL and the date it was retrieved. 5. Extracts are refreshed ahead of time, never while a request is handled. A tool shipped with SPieGeL downloads the vocabularies and writes the extracts. A scheduled job in the CI of the configuration repository runs it and opens a merge request, which the Linked Data team reviews like any other change of configuration. 6. Additional label files may sit next to an extract, for example Dutch labels for external terms, such as those published by OSLO. They take precedence over the extract of the same vocabulary. 7. At start-up SPieGeL builds an index from the extracts: per term, its kind, and its labels and descriptions per language. Looking up a label needs no query. Language follows the tenant's priority list (FR-HTML-10). 8. Shared labels serve presentation only. They are used in HTML, for link texts and, with the descriptions, as explanations of properties. They are not added to RDF responses, which hold only what the data sources return.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One copy of each external vocabulary, maintained in one place, serves every tenant. Stores no longer need to hold external ontologies only for their labels.
  • A build of the configuration is reproducible: it depends on no external site, and every change to a vocabulary's labels is reviewed. Because extracts are configuration, a refresh changes the configuration version, and responses follow (ADR 0020).
  • A refresh can fail when a vocabulary's site is down or no longer negotiates RDF. The previous extract then stays, and the merge request says which vocabulary could not be retrieved.
  • Extracts are small, because they leave out axioms and other languages. Their size, and that of the index in memory, must be checked for large vocabularies such as QUDT.
  • A domain still wins over the shared source, so it can give its own labels for external terms.
  • SPieGeL ships one more tool, next to the context generator of ADR 0017. Both read vocabularies and shapes, and could share code.
  • Labels of resources of other domains stay unsolved until open question 42 is answered: until then their links show the IRI, unless the domain's own store holds a label.

docs.title: 0022. Keep TLS and flood protection at the edge; move the 303, CORS and real rate limits into SPieGeL
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-26

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
In the predecessor, a reverse proxy per domain maps the public host name to the domain, answers /id/ requests with the 303 redirect, and adds an open CORS policy, HSTS and some input filtering (What sits in front of it). The application has its own 303 as well, but public traffic never reaches it. Which of these concerns move into SPieGeL was open question 13. Rate limiting (NFR-OPS-08) is a new concern for the same choice.

Several decisions already point one way:

  • The URI templates are tenant configuration (ADR 0012). A proxy that answers the 303 needs its own copy of them.
  • CORS must be set in exactly one place. If the proxy and the application both add Access-Control-Allow-Origin, the browser receives the header twice and rejects the response. Only SPieGeL knows whether a response is public; from phase 2 some are not (NFR-OPEN-01).
  • TLS ends at the proxy, and HSTS belongs to the host's TLS (request flow, step 0).
  • SPieGeL encodes output and does not filter input by character lists (NFR-SEC-05). It validates what it uses: template variables by pattern (ADR 0012), queries by the query policy (ADR 0011), parameters such as _page (ADR 0016). A content filter at the edge would block legitimate SPARQL, in which <, SELECT or FILTER are normal.

Rate limiting is a real choice. The proxy stops load before any work is done, but knows only addresses: not the tenant, the kind of request or, from phase 2, the caller's identity, and it cannot answer with problem+json. SPieGeL knows all of these, but a flood reaches it first, and its limits must hold across nodes without sticky sessions (NFR-OPS-01, NFR-OPS-08). A counter shared exactly between nodes needs a shared store, such as Redis or Valkey: one more stateful component, and one more thing that can fail. A counter per node, with a share of the limit, needs nothing, but is approximate.

In phase 1 every caller is anonymous, and the proxy is the first defence. SPieGeL's own limits are there to share the data sources fairly, for example so that one client cannot hold every slot for /sparql, not to count exactly.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. SPieGeL answers the 303 for every id URI, from the tenant's URI templates (request flow, step 5). The proxy forwards /id/ requests like any other.
  2. SPieGeL sets the CORS headers, and only SPieGeL. The proxy adds none and removes none.
  3. The proxy terminates TLS and sets HSTS. It passes the original host, scheme and client address in X-Forwarded-* headers. SPieGeL trusts those headers only from the configured addresses of the proxy.
  4. The proxy sets generic limits only: the size of the request, the URL and the headers, connection limits and time-outs. It does not filter on content.
  5. Rate limiting has two layers, each with its own role:
    • the proxy protects against floods, with a generous limit per client address, well above SPieGeL's own limits;
    • SPieGeL sets the real limits: per client, per tenant and per kind of request, with a stricter limit for /sparql, answered with 429, Retry-After and problem+json (request flow, step 3a). The limits are tenant configuration, with shared defaults (ADR 0012).
  6. A client is identified by its address as passed on by the proxy, and from phase 2 by its identity once it is authenticated. Counters never reach a log (ADR 0018).
  7. SPieGeL counts behind a port, RateLimitPort.
    • The first adapter, for phase 1, counts in memory on each node, up to the limit divided by the number of nodes. That number is deployment configuration.
    • A second adapter counts in a shared store, once one exists, for example for the shared cache of ADR 0020 or for limits per identity in phase 2.
    • If the shared store fails, it fails open, falling back to the count per node: a helper component never takes the service down, and a limit remains.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The URI templates, CORS and the limits per tenant live in one place, the tenant configuration, and are tested with SPieGeL. A change to a tenant's limits needs no change at the proxy.
  • The proxy's configuration becomes the same for every tenant: TLS, HSTS, forwarding headers, generic limits and flood protection. A new tenant needs only its host name and certificate there.
  • In phase 1, SPieGeL's limits hold across nodes only approximately: a client whose requests happen to land on one node meets its limit a little earlier. NFR-OPS-08 says so. With autoscaling, the configured number of nodes may differ from the real one for a while; the limit is then briefly too strict or too loose.
  • A flood is stopped at the proxy only above its generous limit. Below it, the load reaches SPieGeL, where the rate limit and the bounded pools of NFR-OPS-02 contain it.
  • Moving to a shared store is a change of adapter, not of the core or the configuration.
  • During migration, the predecessor's proxy rules for the 303, CORS and input filtering must be removed for hosts served by SPieGeL. Otherwise CORS headers appear twice.

docs.title: 0023. Link resources to their event streams from configuration, and serve versions as ordinary resources
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-26

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0006 makes resource endpoints and event streams (LDES) two forms of the same data: SPieGeL serves a resource's current state, an LDES server its history. SPieGeL does not serve streams, but makes them discoverable (FR-ES-01). Open question 30 asked two things: how a resource points to the stream that publishes it, and whether SPieGeL serves the version objects that streams often contain.

Discovery. A domain's dataset description is in DCAT and VoID (FR-META-01), and every page already links to it with rel="describedby" (ADR 0019). A stream can be listed there as a dcat:DataService. That gives a path from a resource to its stream in two steps, but a client must then work out from the DCAT which stream holds which kind of resource.

LDES links only from a stream to its members (tree:member); it has no standard property for the other direction. A stream usually publishes one collection, such as all resources of one type, which matches a URI template or resource type in the tenant configuration (ADR 0012). The IANA link relation collection (RFC 6573) says that "the target is a collection of which the context is a member".

A triple per resource in the data would repeat the same statement millions of times, without a standard property to use. SPieGeL adds no triples of its own to a description's data (ADR 0021).

Versions. LDES members are often version objects with IRIs of their own, related to the resource by dct:isVersionOf. If such an IRI is under a host that SPieGeL serves and cannot be dereferenced, it breaks a basic promise of Linked Data. Serving past states by date, for example with Memento (RFC 7089), would require SPieGeL to understand time and every store to keep the full history of every resource, which is what the stream already offers.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. A domain lists its streams in its dataset description, each as a dcat:DataService with its endpoint and the dataset it serves (FR-META-01). The front page shows them.
  2. A resource links directly to the stream that publishes it. The tenant configuration says, per URI template or resource type, which stream publishes those resources. SPieGeL then sends Link: <stream>; rel="collection" with every format, and shows the link on the HTML page.
  3. The link is configuration, not data. SPieGeL adds no triple to the RDF of the description. The data owner maintains nothing per resource.
  4. Version objects are ordinary resources. If a version IRI matches a URI template and the store holds the version, SPieGeL describes it like any other resource. If the store does not hold it, the answer is 404, as for any unknown resource. Whether a store keeps versions is decided by the loading chain, for example by an LDES client that materialises the stream.
  5. No mechanism of its own for versions. A version links to its resource through dct:isVersionOf in the data, which SPieGeL shows as any link. The versions of a resource are its incoming relations by dct:isVersionOf, available as a paged list (ADR 0015). SPieGeL does not negotiate by date (Memento) and does not reconstruct past states.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A client finds a resource's stream in one step, from any format, and a person sees it on the page. A client that wants the full picture still finds every stream in the dataset description.
  • rel="collection" for an event stream is an interpretation of RFC 6573, not part of the LDES specification. SPieGeL documents it; if LDES later defines a relation of its own, SPieGeL can send both.
  • The configuration must follow the streams: when a stream is added, moved or split, the tenant configuration changes with it. A wrong link is not detected by SPieGeL.
  • Version IRIs on SPieGeL's hosts can be dereferenced wherever the store holds them, with no work in SPieGeL beyond a URI template. A domain that wants this needs a store that keeps versions; a domain that does not, answers 404 for them.
  • The current state in SPieGeL and the latest version in the stream must still agree, as ADR 0006 requires. That stays the responsibility of the loading chain.
  • Anyone who wants the history as a whole, or the state on a given date, replicates the stream. SPieGeL does not compete with the LDES server.

docs.title: 0024. Compact JSON-LD from CONSTRUCT and DESCRIBE with the tenant's context, unless another form is asked for
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-26

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0017 serves descriptions as JSON-LD framed by one generic frame and compacted with a frozen context per tenant. It says nothing about /sparql. A CONSTRUCT or DESCRIBE result is an arbitrary graph without a single subject, so the frame does not apply, but the context still could: it gives short keys and stable shapes without a frame. This was open question 41.

On /sparql the store returns a fixed format, and SPieGeL writes the negotiated one (request flow, steps 5 and 6). JSON-LD is written once the result is complete, within the result limit, so compaction adds processing time but no new limit on size.

JSON-LD 1.1 defines a profile parameter on application/ld+json, by which a client asks for a form: http://www.w3.org/ns/json-ld#expanded, …#compacted, …#flattened or …#framed. A server may ignore it.

Without compaction, a web developer gets full IRIs, unlike what /doc returns. With compaction always, a client that wants expanded JSON-LD has no choice.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. SPieGeL follows the JSON-LD profile parameter for CONSTRUCT and DESCRIBE results on /sparql:

    Asked for Result no profile, or …#compacted compacted with the tenant's current context, referred to by its URI (ADR 0017) …#expanded expanded, without context …#flattened flattened, without context …#framed not supported: compacted, as without a profile

  2. The result stays lossless. A predicate without a term in the context becomes a prefixed name or a full IRI (ADR 0017, decision 5).

  3. The response says which form it has, with the profile in Content-Type, and Vary: Accept.
  4. Compaction happens in the SPARQL adapter, which writes the result. The use case passes it the tenant's context with the handle; the core neither holds nor writes the result (ADR 0010).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A query from a web application returns the same keys as the descriptions on /doc, with no context of its own.
  • Clients that want plain RDF in JSON-LD, such as generic RDF libraries, ask for expanded or flattened, or use another format. Any form is valid JSON-LD, so a client that ignores the profile still gets the same triples.
  • Compaction costs time per response, bounded by the result limit. /sparql is not cached by default, so the cost is paid on every request; it is to be measured in the spike of ADR 0017.
  • The forms are more variants to test, with the same context as the descriptions.
  • Descriptions on /doc remain framed (ADR 0017). Whether they also honour expanded and flattened is not decided here.

docs.title: 0025. Offer federated queries in the portal, run by Comunica in the visitor's browser
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-26

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Integration across domains is left to consumers (ADR 0006): SPieGeL does not join data across domains, and its /sparql refuses SERVICE (ADR 0011). Open question 31 asked whether a federating query engine has a role on the consumer's side, and whether SPieGeL documents or offers one.

Comunica is a query engine for JavaScript (MIT). It answers one SPARQL query over several sources, such as SPARQL endpoints, by splitting it into subqueries per source and joining the results itself; it needs no SERVICE. It runs in the browser, with ready-made builds per major version and per fixed version. Release 5.2 (April 2026) focused on the robustness and performance of federated queries over SPARQL endpoints.

The portal page (FR-HTML-08) on the umbrella domain's host already knows every domain (open question 25), and each domain's dataset description names its SPARQL endpoint (void:sparqlEndpoint, FR-META-01). Public endpoints send Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * (NFR-OPEN-01), which is what a client in the browser needs. Each domain host will have a SPARQL editor (open question 37).

A federated query becomes many requests: per triple pattern and per source, often after an ASK or a count to find out which source can answer. One query in the portal can send tens or hundreds of requests to every domain, and each domain limits each client (ADR 0022). Comunica can retry failed requests (httpRetryCount, httpRetryDelay), set time-outs and use a custom fetch function. Its documentation names no option to honour Retry-After or to bound the number of parallel requests.

A limit that is raised for federation traffic would need to recognise it, for example by a header or user agent, which any client can imitate.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. The portal offers a federated SPARQL editor. The query runs in the visitor's browser, with Comunica. SPieGeL runs no federated query on the server, and /sparql keeps refusing SERVICE.
  2. The sources are the public /sparql endpoints of the domains the portal lists, taken from their dataset descriptions. A visitor may choose a subset. No credentials are sent: federation covers public data only.
  3. It is the same editor as on each domain's host (question 37), with Comunica as its engine instead of a single endpoint.
  4. The portal makes Comunica a polite client, with a fetch function of its own that:
    • sends only a few requests at a time to each domain;
    • on 429 or 503, waits as long as Retry-After says, and then tries again;
    • stops after an overall time-out, which the visitor sees and can cancel sooner.
  5. SPieGeL makes no exception for federation. Its rate limits are the same for every client. The limit for /sparql is chosen with federation in mind, and checked in a spike with typical federated queries.
  6. Comunica is a pinned version, served from the portal's own host, and loaded only when the editor is opened. Nothing is fetched from a third-party CDN at run time. An update is a deliberate change, like any other dependency.
  7. It comes after /sparql, which is phase 2.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• People can ask questions across domains in one place, without installing anything, and the department runs no federation service.
  • ADR 0006 holds: data is joined on the consumer's side, in the consumer's browser.
  • Federated queries are slower than queries on one store, and can be slowed down further by rate limits. The editor says so, and shows progress where Comunica allows it.
  • The polite fetch is a small piece of code to maintain. It also shows other clients how to behave towards SPieGeL's limits.
  • The portal page carries a large script, but only when the editor is opened. The rest of the portal stays readable without JavaScript (NFR-UI-04), and the CSP allows the script from the portal's own host only (NFR-UI-03).
  • A domain that is down or slow delays or fails a federated query. The editor reports which domain did not answer.
  • Federation over private data, with a token per domain, is not offered. It would need a decision of its own.

docs.title: 0026. Draw SPieGeL's boundary by what answers requests, what runs in CI, what holds data, and what runs at the consumer
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-26

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
SPieGeL serves several domains (tenants), each with its own host name, data sources and configuration (FR-MT-01). A growing number of things concern all domains together rather than one:

  • already decided, inside SPieGeL: the portal page on the umbrella domain's host (FR-HTML-08), the shared defaults of the configuration (ADR 0012, ADR 0013), the extracts of external vocabularies (ADR 0021) and the federated SPARQL editor in the portal (ADR 0025);
  • shared infrastructure between nodes: the shared cache (ADR 0020) and the shared counters for rate limits (ADR 0022);
  • tools without a fixed place: the context generator (ADR 0017), the vocabulary extractor (ADR 0021), and the validation of tenant configuration with SHACL in CI (ADR 0012, ADR 0013);
  • published conventions without a fixed place: the configuration vocabulary (https://w3id.org/spiegel/config#), the problem types (https://w3id.org/spiegel/problem/, ADR 0016), the use of rel="collection" for event streams (ADR 0023), and the convention for URIs in other distributions (open question 32);
  • still open: an index of labels across domains (open question 42), full-text search across domains (FR-SRCH-02), the umbrella catalogue that harvests the dataset descriptions (FR-META-01, open question 25), and monitoring across tenants;
  • outside the project, but depended on: the loading chain (open question 15), which also signals each tenant's data version, the LDES servers (ADR 0006), and the identity provider for phase 2.

Without a rule, each of these would be placed case by case: some in the application, some as separate services, some nowhere. A component that holds data from every domain inside SPieGeL would make SPieGeL stateful and a joiner of data across domains, which ADR 0006 leaves to consumers.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. What answers HTTP requests on a tenant's host, from configuration, is part of SPieGeL, in the same artefact. This includes the portal, as the front page of the umbrella domain's tenant, and the federated editor on it. A cross-domain feature that only presents what other tenants publish is a page of a tenant, not a separate service.
  2. What is used to write, check or prepare configuration, and not while a request is handled, is a separate artefact in the same repository: a Maven module spiegel-tools, delivered as a command-line tool. It holds the context generator, the vocabulary extractor and the configuration validator. It shares code with the adapters, such as the configuration model and its SHACL shapes, so that CI and the server check the same rules. The scripts under tools/ in the repository, such as the latency measurement, stay outside the build.
  3. What holds data gathered from several domains is never built or held by SPieGeL. Such an index, of labels or for search across domains, is a store of its own, filled by the loading chain. SPieGeL reads it as an ordinary data source, through DataSourcePort or SearchPort, with the same access levels as any other. Whether such an index is needed is decided per case (open question 42, FR-SRCH-02).
  4. What runs at the consumer is not part of SPieGeL. Query engines, LDES clients and integrations belong to the consumer, even when SPieGeL ships them to the browser, as the portal does with Comunica (ADR 0025).
  5. Defaults have two layers. SPieGeL ships built-in defaults, such as the generic template and the default queries, that make it work without configuration. The organisation's shared defaults, such as the list of external vocabularies and the large properties, live in the configuration repository and are maintained by the Linked Data team (ADR 0013).
  6. Conventions that SPieGeL defines are documented and published with SPieGeL: the configuration vocabulary and its shapes, the problem types, and the link relations it sends. They are versioned with SPieGeL's releases.
  7. Shared infrastructure between nodes is not a domain component. A shared cache or counter store is a deployment choice behind a port (ADR 0020, ADR 0022), not a part of SPieGeL's design. Monitoring dashboards across tenants belong to the platform; SPieGeL provides metrics labelled by tenant (ADR 0018).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• SPieGeL stays a stateless reader: every piece of data it serves comes from a data source or from configuration, and it can be scaled and restarted freely (NFR-OPS-01).
  • The portal and the federated editor need no deployment of their own. A new domain appears in them through configuration only (FR-MT-02).
  • CI and the server use the same configuration model and the same validation, because spiegel-tools and the adapters share code.
  • A cross-domain index is a separate piece of work, with an owner of its own, usually alongside the loading chain. SPieGeL only needs its endpoint in the configuration.
  • Open question 42 is narrowed: SPieGeL will not build a label index itself. The options that remain are copies in each store, a shared label store, reading another tenant's public data source, or the IRI as it is.
  • Several components outside the project (the loading chain, the umbrella catalogue, LDES servers, the identity provider, platform monitoring) need an owner. That is an organisational question, which this decision does not answer.
  • The module structure gains spiegel-tools, which arrives when its first tool is built.

docs.title: NNNN. Title in the imperative
docs.text:
• Status: Proposed | Accepted | Superseded by NNNN
  • Date: YYYY-MM-DD

docs.title: Context
docs.text: What is the issue that motivates this decision? Which forces are at play?

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: What we decided, stated plainly.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: What becomes easier or harder as a result, including the drawbacks we accept.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
This section collects the analysis behind SPieGeL. It describes what the predecessor platform does, what its successor must do, what already exists elsewhere, and how we intend to build it.

The analysis is a snapshot. It records what we found and why we concluded what we did. Decisions taken on the basis of it are recorded separately as architecture decision records.

docs.title: Reading guide
docs.text: Chapter Question it answers Start here if you are… 1. Context Why does SPieGeL exist, and what is in scope? new to the project 2. Current platform What does the predecessor do today, exactly? migrating behaviour or checking compatibility 3. Requirements What must SPieGeL do, and how important is each item? planning work or writing tests 4. Landscape What existing open-source software does similar things? asking "why not reuse X?" 5. Architecture How is SPieGeL structured? writing code 6. Open questions What is still undecided? looking for something to resolve

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• British English throughout.
  • Predecessor means the NetKernel-based Linked Open Data platform that SPieGeL replaces.
  • Requirement priorities use MoSCoW: Must, Should, Could, Won't (this time).
  • Requirement identifiers (FR-…, NFR-…) are stable. Do not renumber them; deprecate instead.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text: Questions that the analysis could not settle. When one is answered, record the answer as an ADR and link it here, rather than deleting the question.

docs.title: Product and scope
docs.text:
1. One multi-tenant service, or one service per domain? SPieGeL's design assumes one stateless multi-tenant service (FR-MT-01). Newer domains, however, use small purpose-built services. Which model does the organisation want for the long term?
  2. Are the non-public access levels still used? The X-Cite project assumes authentication is "no longer used in practice". If that is true for every domain, phase 2 can drop access control. Usage data per domain should settle this before FR-AC-01 to 03 are built.
  3. Are reconciliation, Linked Data Fragments and the alternative search back ends used by anyone? They exist in the predecessor but are not routed.
  4. Is keyword search still needed? The X-Cite project grades full-text search as won't; the predecessor offers it per domain.
  5. Should the restricted HTML view of incoming relations exist? The predecessor intended it but never had it in effect (see Request flows).
  6. Is the dba domain still maintained, or can it be published as a static snapshot? Answered: the domain is fully static. It can be published from a read-only snapshot, without a store that is loaded continuously (see question 29).
  7. Which consumers rely on the predecessor's URIs and formats? For example dataset catalogues and metadata portals that link to it.

docs.title: Front end
docs.text:
1. Do the omgeving-ld browser components stay? Answered by ADR 0005: no. They are replaced by Flux components where those exist (accordion, rich data table, pager, map, properties), and by new components built to Flux's conventions where they do not: the hierarchy tree, incoming relations, the collection table and the SPARQL editor (FR-HTML-05; see Design system: Flux). Still open: must the same-origin /sparql and the HTML conventions in Client components (ld-subject, the .rq templates under /queries/) stay for a transition period, for pages elsewhere that still embed the old components?
  2. Which template engine for HTML? The design system is decided: Flux (ADR 0005). The template engine must emit custom elements, slots and attributes cleanly, and encode output by context (NFR-SEC-05). It must also work without Spring, because spiegel-adapter-html has no Spring dependency (ADR 0004), and support translation files (FR-HTML-12) and reusable fragments, such as the RDF term. FreeMarker and Pebble do not encode by context, which leaves Thymeleaf (templates loaded at run time) and JTE (templates compiled, type-safe). Which of the two fits depends on whether tenants write templates of their own or configure their layout (FR-HTML-03). On hold: the question waits for question 40, because a page built in the browser needs no template engine on the server.
  3. Where are the domain-specific explorer scripts for imjv, cbb and dba, and are they still needed?
  4. How are presentation rules expressed? The predecessor chooses blocks and components with XSLT rules by type and predicate (see Data-dependent HTML rendering). FR-HTML-06 makes these rules configuration. Candidates: rules attached to profiles (as in Prez), viewers per URI template (as in ELDA), or a small rule format of our own.
  5. Under which licence is Flux published, and can external contributors build SPieGeL? The Flux repository has no licence file, and its packages come from the department's Artifactory, not from the public npm registry. SPieGeL is public and MIT-licensed, and its release would bundle Flux code (see Design system: Flux).
  6. Do the new Linked Data components live in SPieGeL or in Flux? A resource description, a hierarchy tree, incoming relations, a collection table, a geometry map and a SPARQL editor are needed (see Design system: Flux). Contributing them to Flux makes them reusable but ties their release to Flux's. Answered by ADR 0014: what is specific to Linked Data stays in SPieGeL; what turns out to be generic, such as paging on the server or WKT input for the map, is offered to Flux. The hierarchy waits for question 39.
  7. Do interactive components query /sparql from the browser, or call small JSON endpoints? The predecessor's components build SPARQL in the browser. Server-side endpoints per function keep queries configurable, cacheable and authorised (NFR-SEC-03, NFR-SEC-04). A map of a resource's own geometries needs neither, because its data is in the page. The Flux team assumes that long lists of incoming relations are paged like the RDF, as paged lists with their own URI; FR-RA-07 only covers the subject's own properties, so that is to be decided here as well. A map of many resources (for example all members of a collection) does need a follow-up request. With /sparql, the GeoSPARQL 1.1 function geof:asGeoJSON could return GeoJSON directly, but support differs between stores and its output is always WGS84. Answered by ADR 0015: neither. The components request paged lists, which are Linked Data resources with their own URI (?_property=…, ?_inverse=…), as JSON-LD with a fixed @context; the queries stay on the server, cached and authorised.
  8. Where does the portal discover domains? From the tenant configuration (always complete for SPieGeL's own tenants, but blind to domains published elsewhere), or from the actual publication, for example a dcat:Catalog per domain in the umbrella open data catalogue (always in step with what is published, but it requires that catalogue to describe every domain), or both (FR-HTML-08). And which properties describe a domain in the catalogue: title, description, host name, SPARQL endpoint?
  9. Which languages does the interface offer? Dutch only, Dutch and English, or also French and German (FR-HTML-12)? Do Flux and Digitaal Vlaanderen's global header support the same languages, and who maintains the translations?

  10. Do we adopt, fork or build the SPARQL editor? @sib-swiss/sparql-editor (MIT) is a web component built on YASGUI that autocompletes classes and properties from an endpoint's VoID description, lists its SHACL example queries and reads its prefixes from sh:prefix, all metadata that SPieGeL publishes (FR-META-03, FR-SPARQL-04). See UniProt. Adopting it would save building the editor, the component with the least Flux support (see Design system). Points to check before choosing:

    • Content Security Policy: whether the component and the editor library it uses work without inline scripts and inline styles (NFR-UI-03).
    • House style and accessibility: whether its look can follow Flux, and whether it meets the accessibility guidelines that come with Flux (NFR-UI-01, NFR-UI-02).
    • Results: whether it shows results itself, or SPieGeL renders them with clickable IRIs and labels in vl-rich-data-table (FR-SPARQL-03, FR-HTML-10).
    • Languages: whether its interface texts can be translated into Dutch (FR-HTML-12, question 27).
    • Load on the endpoint: its autocompletion queries /sparql from the browser. They count towards the rate limits (NFR-OPS-08), and relate to question 24.

    • Build and supply: whether it is bundled in SPieGeL's own front-end build rather than loaded from a CDN, and how much it depends on one small team at SIB.

    • Keyboard: a code editor uses Tab for indenting, so keyboard users need a documented way out of it (WCAG 2.1.2, raised by the Flux team).

    • Federation: whether its query engine can be replaced by Comunica, so that the same editor serves the portal's federated queries (ADR 0025).

    The options are to use it as it is, to fork it with Flux styling, or to build an editor on YASGUI or another editor library directly.

  11. Does the predecessor's "Browse dataset" tree work? The XSLT renders <ld-dataset> for catalogues and datasets, but omgeving-ld 1.7.27 does not register the component and its bundles do not contain it (see Client components). A check on a live catalogue page settles whether users have this tree today, which matters for the migration (see question 7), not for SPieGeL's requirement (FR-HTML-05).

  12. How are data structures made visible? Flux 2.21.0 offers vl-cascader, a drilldown with a breadcrumb that loads each level on demand, as a base for the hierarchies of concept schemes and catalogues (FR-HTML-05). Rather than choosing between a drilldown and an expanded tree now, the Flux team has been asked to think about how data structures in general can be made visible: hierarchies, collections, and perhaps the structure of a domain's data (FR-HTML-15). Until it answers, vl-cascader is the candidate (see Design system: Flux, ADR 0014).

  13. Is HTML rendered on the server, or built in the browser by a JavaScript one-page application? The Flux team suggested a one-page application instead of server-side templates, and is investigating whether it is possible and desirable, given how much logic it moves into JavaScript. The analysis so far assumes rendering on the server, with Flux components that upgrade in the browser (Design system: Flux, constraint 2). The investigation should answer how a one-page application meets what is already decided:

    • NFR-UI-04: the title, properties, links and alternate formats are readable without JavaScript. The analysis ruled out data.vlaanderen.be's approach for this reason (Design system: Flux).
    • ADR 0007: subject pages are the landing pages for links from GIS layers, downloads and APIs, and must work at once for people, crawlers, link previews and web archives.
    • FR-HTML-04: the subject IRI, <link rel="alternate"> and the embedded JSON-LD are in the HTML as sent.
    • ADR 0014: the resource description and the RDF term are templates on the server. In a one-page application they become components, so seven components instead of three or four.
    • NFR-PERF-01: a description from the cache within 50 ms on the server. In a one-page application the visitor also waits for the bundle and a second request for the data.
    • ADR 0019: search engines index reliably what is in the HTML as sent: the schema.org block, Open Graph tags and canonical links (FR-HTML-16, FR-HTML-17).
    • Rendering on the server with Lit needs Node.js, a second runtime next to the Java server.

    What a one-page application would gain: no templating in Java, one code base in the Flux team's own stack, richer interaction, and a server that only serves RDF and JSON-LD, which fits the paged lists of ADR 0015. A middle way keeps the content rendered on the server and moves more of the interaction into JavaScript components. Question 9 waits for this answer.

docs.title: URI policy
docs.text:
1. Where does the list of valid concepts per domain come from? In the predecessor it is deployment configuration. Options: SPieGeL's tenant configuration, the data itself (co:Collection resources), or the vocabulary projects. Answered by ADR 0012: from the data. Template variables are typed by a pattern; a value that matches is looked up, and a negative result is cached per data version. A tenant that wants a closed list writes it as a pattern.
  2. Which domains publish legislative resources that need ELI paths (FR-URI-05)?

docs.title: Architecture and operations
docs.text:
1. Which edge concerns move into SPieGeL? The 303 redirect, CORS, HSTS and input filtering are currently handled by the reverse proxy. Rate limiting (NFR-OPS-08) is a new concern for the same choice. At the edge it protects SPieGeL before any work is done, but it only knows addresses. That is enough for public access, which is unauthenticated, but not for limits per authenticated client. In SPieGeL it can also limit per authenticated client, per tenant and per kind of request, but it needs a counter shared between nodes. See Request flow. Answered by ADR 0022: the proxy keeps TLS, HSTS, generic limits and flood protection per address; SPieGeL answers the 303, sets CORS and enforces the real rate limits, counting per node in phase 1 behind a RateLimitPort.
  2. Does the core use Jena's model types, or its own RDF abstraction? See Hexagonal design. Answered by ADR 0010: the core uses Jena's graph types from jena-core, and nothing from jena-arq.
  3. Is the data loading (ETL) chain in scope of this project at all, or a separate line of work?
  4. Which configuration mechanism in production? For example environment variables, mounted files or a configuration server. Answered by ADR 0013: a versioned artefact built from one central configuration repository, validated in CI, mounted read-only and rolled out with a rolling restart; credentials come from the platform's secret store.
  5. Fork pull requests: the internal CI does not build pull requests from external forks. When external contributors appear, do we add a minimal public CI for them?
  6. Are redirects for moved or retired URIs data or configuration? Trifid reads them from the store, modelled with the W3C HTTP vocabulary, so data owners can manage them without a deployment (see Trifid code review). The alternative is SPieGeL's tenant configuration. This affects NFR-OPEN-02. Partly answered by FR-URI-11: both, by scale. A single URI is data in the store, a whole URI pattern or host name is configuration. The data describes the fact (dct:isReplacedBy, a status, a tombstone) rather than the HTTP response, because the HTTP in RDF vocabulary is a W3C note that is no longer maintained, and the fact is also useful to RDF consumers. Still open: the exact properties for a tombstone, and whether the domains' existing validity properties are enough for FR-URI-09.
  7. Hand-written queries, generated queries, or both? Prez generates each description query from a SHACL shape per profile; SPieGeL's requirements assume query files (FR-RA-02). Generating the simple cases and keeping files for tuned ones is a possible middle way (see Prez code review). Answered by ADR 0012: default .rq templates shipped with SPieGeL, replaced or extended by hand-written files. Generation from SHACL may come later, as an adapter that supplies QuerySpecs.
  8. Do we adopt the Linked Data API vocabulary for tenant configuration? ELDA's model (item and list endpoints, item templates, selectors, viewers, formatters) covers most of FR-URI-01, FR-RA-01 and FR-HTML-03, and comes with a published vocabulary (see ELDA code review). The alternatives are a subset of it, extended with profiles and access levels, or SPieGeL's own format. Answered by ADR 0012: no. The configuration is Turtle in SPieGeL's own small vocabulary, which reuses api:uriTemplate and api:itemTemplate along with prof:, sh:, dcat: and void: terms.
  9. Where do the labels of external vocabularies come from? Either every store holds the external ontologies its data uses, which is simple for SPieGeL but means loading and maintaining the same ontologies in every store (a job for the loading chain, question 15). Or SPieGeL has one shared vocabulary source for all tenants, as Prez bundles labels of common vocabularies (Prez code review), which loads each ontology once. Or both, in that order (FR-HTML-11). A fourth option, fetching an unknown vocabulary from the web while a request is handled, is ruled out: it is slow, depends on third-party sites being up, and conflicts with NFR-SEC-06 (SPieGeL only contacts configured sources). Loading vocabularies from the web ahead of time, into the shared source, remains possible as part of maintaining it. Answered by ADR 0021: the domain's own store first, then extracts of external vocabularies in the configuration: only kinds, labels and descriptions, refreshed ahead of time by a CI job and reviewed. Labels of resources of other domains are question 42.

  10. Materialise or translate non-RDF sources (FR-DS-02)? Answered by ADR 0009: relational sources that must be current are translated per request by Ontop, running as a separate SPARQL endpoint; everything else is materialised with RML in the loading chain. Still open: which sources need to be current to the second. The analysis that led to the decision follows. With materialisation, an RML processor (for example RMLMapper or RMLStreamer) generates RDF into a store in the loading chain (question 15). SPieGeL then only reads that store through its SPARQL adapter, and needs no extra adapter. With translation per request (a virtual knowledge graph), queries are rewritten against the source itself, so data is always current, but tool support is narrower: as far as we know it exists mainly for R2RML over relational databases (for example Ontop, which can itself expose a SPARQL endpoint). RML covers more source types (CSV, JSON, XML, Web APIs), but every RML processor we looked at (October 2026) materialises; none rewrites queries per request:

    • RMLMapper (Java 21, MIT, used as a command-line tool or a library) reads relational databases through JDBC. Its database access (the dataio library) only accepts a fixed list of databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle, IBM DB2, H2, Denodo, Athena, Snowflake). Trino is not on it, so Trino would need a change to that library. It also loads the whole query result into memory as CSV before mapping it. It depends on both Jena and RDF4J, and its support for the Community Group's RML modules is still partial.
    • RMLStreamer (Apache Flink) reads JDBC, Kafka and TCP streams, but its last release dates from 2023.
    • CARML (Java, RDF4J, Project Reactor) has no relational source at all: only CSV, JSON and XML.
    • Morph-KGC (Python) covers the most databases, through SQLAlchemy rather than JDBC, and already supports RML 1.2. It can only run as a separate step in the loading chain, not inside SPieGeL.

    So translation per request means R2RML and a tool such as Ontop; RML in practice means materialisation. Which sources need to be current to the second, and which can be loaded periodically? 29. Which kind of store serves which access level? Today the domains live in Virtuoso, which enforces access levels itself: each level's account can only read the graphs that level may see (FR-AC-03, NFR-SEC-02). Faster or cheaper stores do not offer that:

    • QLever (C++, Apache 2.0) is a candidate to replace Virtuoso. It supports SPARQL 1.1 with named graphs, has its own text search (ql:contains-word), and builds its index in a separate step. It has no users or graph permissions: one access token only unlocks administrative calls, such as longer timeouts.
    • HDT is a compressed, read-only RDF file that can be queried without loading it into a database. Through hdt-jena (LGPL) SPieGeL could query it in-process, without a separate server; qEndpoint and Fuseki can serve it as an endpoint. HDT has no named graphs, and hdt-java was last released in 2023.
    • Oxigraph can serve a store it has loaded in a read-only mode.
    • Neo4j is not a SPARQL store and keeps named graphs only partly; it fits only as a public artefact built by the loading chain, for consumers (question 33).

    Access is restricted per triple, not per resource: a person's employment by a company can be public while the person's name is not. There are four ways to combine such stores with access levels:

    1. One cumulative store per level. Each level gets its own copy, with its own graphs and those of the levels below. Separation is physical and queries do not change, but public data is duplicated in every copy. For a large QLever index, every extra level is another full index to build and store.
    2. One file per level, combined per request. Each level gets its own HDT file, without overlap. SPieGeL builds a Jena union of the files the caller may see, so joins across levels still work. This only works in-process: with separate servers it becomes federation, which makes joins slow and complex.
    3. One store with named graphs, restricted by rewriting queries. Workable for SPieGeL's own queries, but risky for /sparql, where every FROM, FROM NAMED, GRAPH and SERVICE must be checked or rejected. One missed construct leaks data, so this is weaker than NFR-SEC-02 requires. Ruled out by ADR 0011: SPieGeL never rewrites queries, and a store without graph permissions serves one access level only.
    4. Split on authentication. Anonymous requests go to derived stores built only from public graphs: for example HDT for /doc and QLever for /sparql. Authenticated requests stay on Virtuoso with today's accounts. No security has to be rebuilt, and the derived stores hold nothing sensitive, which also limits the damage of a configuration error. For an authenticated /doc request, the description can be merged from the public store and a query on the non-public graphs alone, because each query already names its own data source (see Request flow).

    Option 4 fits when most data and traffic are public, and the non-public part is small. It moves the security boundary to the loading chain (question 15). The public export must start from an explicit allowlist of graphs, never from "everything except the non-public ones". A check, for example a SHACL shape or a query for forbidden predicates, must reject any artefact that contains non-public data. Personal data such as names then stays in Virtuoso alone (ADR 0018, NFR-PRIV-01), so a deletion request does not have to be traced through derived artefacts and their releases. Labels of linked resources follow the same rule: for anonymous callers they come from the public store only. If Elasticsearch ever returns (FR-DS-03), it needs a separate index per level rather than a level field and a filter, because suggestions, highlighting and aggregations can leak values.

    A static domain such as dba (question 6) can be served entirely from a snapshot. Open points: which domains hold non-public data at all (question 2), and whether SPieGeL needs a kind of data source other than a SPARQL endpoint, such as an HDT file read in-process (FR-DS-01 only covers endpoints). 30. How do resources and their event streams meet? Two points follow from ADR 0006. First, discovery: a resource needs a way to point to the stream that publishes it, for example a Link header or a triple, and a domain needs a way to list its streams, for example as a DCAT data service in its dataset description (FR-ES-01). Second, versions: LDES members are often version objects with IRIs of their own (dct:isVersionOf the resource). Should SPieGeL dereference those IRIs, and serve past states of a resource, or only the current state? Answered by ADR 0023: the dataset description lists each stream as a dcat:DataService, and the tenant configuration names the stream per URI template or resource type, which SPieGeL sends as Link: <stream>; rel="collection" and shows in HTML. Version objects are ordinary resources: described when the store holds them, with no mechanism of their own and no Memento. 31. Does a federating query engine have a role on the consumer's side? Integration across domains and stores is left to consumers (ADR 0006). A query engine such as Comunica can query several SPARQL endpoints, files and streams in one query. Do we document or offer such a set-up, for example in the SPARQL editor (FR-SPARQL-03)? Answered by ADR 0025: the portal offers a federated SPARQL editor over the domains' public /sparql endpoints, run by Comunica in the visitor's browser, with a polite fetch that bounds parallel requests and honours Retry-After. SPieGeL runs no federation on the server and makes no exception in its rate limits. 32. Where is the convention for URIs in other distributions documented, and who owns it? ADR 0007 asks GIS layers, downloads and APIs to carry each thing's URI. They need a shared convention: the attribute name (a gml:id cannot hold a URI), and how a feature in OGC API Features links to it. Does that belong to the Flemish URI standard, to OSLO, or to the department's own GIS guidelines? And which layers come first, for example the river segments? 33. Does Neo4j have a role for certain use cases? Neo4j is a property graph database, queried with Cypher. As a store for SPieGeL itself it fits poorly, mostly for reasons already in the requirements:

    • It has no SPARQL. Data sources are SPARQL endpoints (FR-DS-01), queries are .rq files under version control (FR-RA-02), and every domain offers a public SPARQL 1.1 endpoint with the standard result formats (FR-SPARQL-01, FR-SPARQL-02). Neo4j could therefore never be a tenant's only store: /sparql still needs a triple store, so Neo4j would always come in addition to Virtuoso or QLever, never instead of them. A Neo4j adapter behind the data source port is possible in the hexagonal design, but tenants would then maintain their queries in two languages, which undermines the idea that a new kind of resource needs only configuration. The port also assumes RDF results (see question 14), so the adapter would have to translate property graph results back to RDF.
    • The data model does not map without loss. RDF reaches Neo4j through the neosemantics plugin (n10s). It imports and exports Turtle, N-Triples, JSON-LD, RDF/XML, TriG and N-Quads, and supports SHACL validation and simple inference. The weak points are what SPieGeL relies on:
      • Named graphs. N-Quads can be imported, but by default n10s keeps only the triple, not the graph IRI. An experimental procedure annotates nodes with their graph IRI, so that the same resource can become several nodes; according to the Neo4j community forum it is limited and not maintained. SPieGeL's access levels rest on named graphs (question 29).
      • Language tags, datatypes, blank nodes and Skolem IRIs. Choosing a label by language priority and showing datatypes (FR-HTML-10), stable Skolem IRIs (FR-URI-04) and nested blank nodes (FR-RA-04) have to be imitated in a property graph. n10s can approach this by configuration, but a lossless round trip RDF → Neo4j → RDF would have to be proven and kept under test, with no functional gain.
      • Support status. n10s is a Neo4j Labs project, not a supported product. It runs only on self-hosted Neo4j (Community and Enterprise), not on the Aura cloud service.
    • Access levels would need a new design. Today Virtuoso enforces the access levels with one read-only account per level, which can only read that level's graphs (NFR-SEC-02). Neo4j's fine-grained permissions on labels, relationship types and properties are, as far as we know, part of the commercial Enterprise edition only. The graph-based model would have to be translated into those permissions, and access is restricted per triple (question 29), which maps badly onto nodes and properties. That is a new security design with new risks, while question 29 leans towards an option that rebuilds no security.
    • Its strengths matter little to SPieGeL. Neo4j has full-text and vector indexes and is strong at traversals. But keyword search uses the data source's own full-text index (FR-SRCH-01), which Virtuoso and QLever have; hierarchies and collections (FR-HTML-05) work with SPARQL property paths; and a description is bounded to its subject (FR-RA-06), so deep traversals are not part of SPieGeL's core task. A vector index matters for LLM use cases such as GraphRAG, which are not in SPieGeL's scope (assisted query building is won't).

    Neo4j may still be worth investigating beside SPieGeL, for use cases where a property graph is stronger than SPARQL: graph algorithms (paths, centrality, communities, for example networks of companies, permits and sites), graph data science, visual exploration of a network, GraphRAG, or data that a source system already keeps in Neo4j. Ways to connect it, none of which makes Neo4j a SPieGeL store:

    1. Neo4j as a derived artefact of the loading chain. Like an HDT file or a QLever index in option 4 of question 29, the loading chain builds a Neo4j database from an allowlist of public graphs. A separate application uses it. SPieGeL does not change, the security boundary stays in the loading chain, and the URIs in the nodes link back to the subject pages (ADR 0007). This is a decision for the loading chain (question 15) and for a consumer application (ADR 0006, question 31), not for SPieGeL's choice of store.
    2. Neo4j as a source. A source system that already keeps its data in Neo4j exports it to RDF (with n10s), and the result is loaded into the triple store, like the materialised non-RDF sources of question 28.
    3. Neo4j read live as RDF. n10s can also return RDF from Cypher over HTTP (to be checked). A tenant could then read a description from Neo4j as RDF without a Cypher adapter in the core. This still needs a SPARQL store for /sparql, and queries in Cypher. It is the least attractive option, to keep only if a concrete use case needs live data from Neo4j.

    Open points: which use cases exist in the department, and whether one of them needs Neo4j rather than a SPARQL store with its own analysis tools. Partly answered by ADR 0008: Neo4j is not a data source for SPieGeL, and a public Neo4j database built by the loading chain remains possible for consumers. Option 3 is therefore ruled out unless a later ADR supersedes 0008. 34. How can applications with a language model (LLM) use the published data? Such applications, for example question answering or GraphRAG, are built on top of the published data, outside SPieGeL, like the consumers of ADR 0006. Three building blocks fit SPieGeL's design without changing it:

    1. Text to SPARQL. A language model translates a question into a SPARQL query on a domain's public /sparql endpoint (FR-SPARQL-01). The domain's description of its own structure gives the model the schema as context: its vocabularies (FR-URI-03), and the SHACL shapes and Data Cube structure definitions (qb:DataStructureDefinition) that several domains already define in advance, such as the cubes of imjv. Where none exist, the structure can be derived from the data itself (FR-HTML-15). A domain's example queries, which pair a question in plain language with its correct SPARQL (FR-SPARQL-04), are ready-made examples for the model. This is the RDF counterpart of Neo4j's Text2CypherRetriever.
    2. Vector search as an entry point. Embeddings of the labels and descriptions of resources are kept in a separate vector index, with the URI as key. A question finds a few URIs by vector search. From those URIs, the application fetches the description and the neighbours through SPieGeL (/doc/… in JSON-LD or Turtle) or through SPARQL. This is the pattern of Neo4j's VectorCypherRetriever, with URIs and SPARQL instead. Only the vector index is new; it is a derived artefact of the loading chain (question 15), like the Neo4j database of question 33.
    3. Sources in every answer. Every resource has a dereferenceable URI, so an answer can link to the subject pages it is based on. ADR 0007 already makes those pages the landing page for links from elsewhere. This makes answers explainable, which is an advantage over retrieval from plain text.

    Points of attention:

    • Access levels are the main risk. Access is restricted per triple, so a language model layer runs on public data only, at least at first: the public derived stores of option 4 of question 29. The vector index follows the same rule, or it can leak labels and values, for the same reason as an Elasticsearch index.
    • Costly queries. Generated queries on /sparql need the same protection as any other client: the bounded concurrency per data source (NFR-OPS-02) and rate limiting per client (NFR-OPS-08).
    • Languages. The embeddings must handle Dutch labels, and English ones where a domain offers them (question 27).

    Open points: whether the department wants such an application, who would build and run it, and whether SPieGeL itself should offer anything for it, such as assisted query building in the SPARQL editor (graded won't in the traceability matrix). 35. Which vocabulary describes the pages of a large property (FR-RA-07)? Two candidates: Answered by ADR 0015: Hydra, with pages of 100 by default ordered by IRI, a bounded count cached per data version, and lists addressed by query parameters on the subject's doc URI.

    • Hydra: a page is a hydra:PartialCollectionView of a hydra:Collection, with hydra:first, hydra:next and hydra:last, and optionally hydra:totalItems. Simple, widely known, and made for exactly this. The specification is a Community Group draft that has hardly moved in recent years.
    • TREE: pages are nodes linked by relations (tree:relation, tree:node). It is the basis of LDES, which Digitaal Vlaanderen and OSLO use, so a client that reads event streams (ADR 0006) already knows it. It is designed for fragmenting large collections by a value, such as time, and is heavier than needed for "the next 100 members".

    Recommendation: Hydra, because the pages of FR-RA-07 are plain, ordered lists and Hydra describes them directly. TREE remains the vocabulary for event streams. Open points: the default page size, whether pages show a total count (a COUNT is costly on a large store, so at most cached), and whether a page has its own URI under the resource or is a profile of it (FR-CN-03). 36. What are the predecessor's actual load and response times? The throughput target (NFR-PERF-04) is relative to the peak load per tenant, and the store choice (question 29) needs a baseline. From the predecessor's access logs: requests per second at peak, per domain and per kind of request (/doc, /sparql, front page), and the share of each media type. Its response times can be measured from outside with the measurement script and the same requests as on candidate stores. Partly answered on Performance and availability: a 48-minute sample of the predecessor's own log gives about one /doc request per second at a median of 4 s, with most of the time spent above the store. Two complete days of the umbrella domain's proxy log show low external traffic (a few thousand requests a day) and an availability of about 97 %. Still open: the same for the other domains and over several weeks (the log export stops at 10,000 rows, so counts per day, path and status are better aggregated in the central logging itself); response times measured from now on; and whether most of the predecessor's requests for algemeen come from inside, from other domains resolving labels. 41. Is JSON-LD from CONSTRUCT on /sparql compacted with the tenant's context? ADR 0017 frames and compacts descriptions. A CONSTRUCT or DESCRIBE result has no single subject, so the frame does not apply, but the tenant's context could still give it short keys and stable shapes. Without it, the result is plain JSON-LD with full IRIs, the same on every tenant. Compacting needs the whole result in memory, which the result limit bounds; JSON-LD is not streamed either way (see Request flow). A client that wants other keys can compact the result itself with its own context. Answered by ADR 0024: SPieGeL follows the JSON-LD profile parameter. Without one, or with compacted, the result is compacted with the tenant's context; expanded and flattened are served as asked; framed is not supported. 42. Where do the labels of resources of other domains come from? Data often links to resources of another tenant, such as a concept from a code list of algemeen on an IMJV page. FR-HTML-10 shows such a link by its label only if the domain's own store holds one; otherwise the IRI is shown. ADR 0021 does not cover this: these labels change with the other tenant's data, and that data has its own access levels. The options are: the loading chain copies the labels into each store that links to them (question 15); SPieGeL looks them up in the other tenant's data source, at the public level only, as a configured label source; one shared label store, fed by the loading chain; or the IRI as it is. An index built and held by SPieGeL itself is ruled out by ADR 0026. The predecessor's logs suggest that resolving such labels causes much of its load on algemeen (question 36, Performance and availability). 43. How does an HTTP cache in front of SPieGeL cache negotiated responses? /doc/x with Accept: text/turtle and /doc/x.ttl have the same body; the negotiated response adds Vary: Accept and a Content-Location that points to /doc/x.ttl (feature 001, AC-3.7 and AC-3.8). SPieGeL's own cache does not depend on the format, because it holds the description, not its serialisation (ADR 0020). A proxy or CDN, however, keys on the URL and, through Vary: Accept, on the raw Accept string. Browsers and crawlers send many different strings that lead to the same format, so it stores many copies of one representation. The options are: - Negotiate in SPieGeL only, as now: correct, but a cache in front hits less often on negotiated URLs. - Negotiate at the edge and rewrite internally to the suffix URL, as the Flux team suggests: the cache then holds one copy per format. Negotiation (quality values, SPieGeL's order of preference, 406) then exists twice, and the edge cannot take over the fallback from RDF/XML to the next format (AC-3.15), which depends on the data. - Cache only the suffix URLs at the edge, and pass negotiated requests through to SPieGeL, or cache them briefly.

    This belongs with caching (feature 002) and the edge concerns of ADR 0022. It does not change feature 001.

docs.title: The predecessor
docs.text:
Since the early 2010s, the Flemish Government's Department of Environment and Spatial Development has published environmental and planning data as Linked Open Data. A single platform serves several data domains, each on its own host name (for example data.imjv.omgeving.vlaanderen.be). For every resource it offers:

  • an identifier (/id/…) that redirects with 303 See Other to a document (/doc/…);
  • the document itself, as HTML for people and as RDF (Turtle, RDF/XML, N-Triples, JSON-LD) for machines;
  • vocabulary pages (/ns/…) for the domain ontologies;
  • a public SPARQL endpoint, keyword search, and an HTML front end that queries that endpoint from the browser.

The platform runs on NetKernel, a resource-oriented computing runtime. NetKernel is no longer actively developed. Much of the platform's behaviour lives in Groovy scripts, FreeMarker templates, XSLT and an XML query catalogue rather than in compiled, tested code. That makes it hard to maintain, and hard to change with confidence.

See Current platform for the full picture.

docs.title: Why a new product rather than a port
docs.text:
A one-to-one port to another runtime would carry over the predecessor's weaknesses: business logic hidden in configuration, routes generated at runtime from environment variables, and behaviour that differs from what the configuration suggests. The analysis showed several places where the intended behaviour and the actual behaviour diverge (see Request flows).

SPieGeL therefore starts from the intended behaviour, expressed as requirements, and implements it as an explicit, tested domain model inside a hexagonal architecture.

docs.title: Why open source
docs.text: Publishing Linked Data with content negotiation, a URI policy and access control is not specific to one department. Other public bodies in the Flemish OSLO and European SEMIC ecosystems face the same problem. Existing open-source tools cover parts of it, but none covers the combination we need (see Landscape). Building SPieGeL in the open lets others reuse it and contribute to it.

docs.title: X-Cite
docs.text: SPieGeL replaces and improves the NetKernel-based platform in line with the requirements of the X-Cite project. X-Cite describes simulation models and datasets with metadata and publishes them as DCAT catalogues, for which it needs a Linked Data service. Its requirements for that service overlap strongly with the needs of the predecessor's successor, so SPieGeL serves both. The X-Cite requirements are traced in Traceability, and the phasing is described in Scope.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Access level A classification of data by sensitivity. The predecessor uses five levels: public, internal, confidential, secret and top secret. A user's level is derived from roles in an identity token. Public, the lowest level, is the level of an unauthenticated client. Content negotiation The HTTP mechanism by which one URI returns different representations, chosen by the client's Accept header. See RFC 9110 §12. Content negotiation by profile Negotiating not only the format but also the profile of a representation, such as a lighter or richer description, or the same data in another model. See the W3C draft Content Negotiation by Profile. Data source A store that SPieGeL reads from. Initially a SPARQL endpoint; later possibly a relational database exposed as a SPARQL endpoint by Ontop through an R2RML mapping. Other non-RDF sources (files, Web APIs) reach SPieGeL only after an RML processor has loaded them into a store. Dereference To look up a URI over HTTP and get something useful back. Domain (also tenant) A coherent body of published data with its own host name, data source and URI space, for example imjv (the Integrated Environmental Annual Report). ELI European Legislation Identifier. A URI scheme and ontology for legislation and legal decisions, with its own hierarchical path structure. Event stream (also LDES) A Linked Data Event Stream: an append-only collection of versions of resources, fragmented so that a client can replicate it and stay in sync. Complementary to SPieGeL's resource endpoints, which serve the current state (see ADR 0006). Hexagonal architecture (also ports and adapters) An architecture in which the domain core depends only on interfaces (ports). Technology-specific code (adapters) implements or calls those interfaces. See Hexagonal design. id / doc / ns The three URI types of the Flemish URI standard for data. id identifies a thing, doc is the web document about it, and ns is a vocabulary namespace. A request for an id URI is answered with 303 See Other to the matching doc URI. Predecessor The NetKernel-based Linked Open Data platform that SPieGeL replaces. Profile A named specification that a representation conforms to, for example "summary" or "full", or "Data Cube" versus "SOSA observation". R2RML RDB to RDF Mapping Language. A W3C Recommendation (2012) for exposing relational data as RDF. Generalised by RML. Ontop uses R2RML to translate SPARQL queries into SQL per request. RML RDF Mapping Language. A declarative language for generating RDF from heterogeneous sources: relational databases, CSV, JSON, XML, Web APIs and streams. It generalises R2RML and is specified in modules (RML-Core, RML-IO, RML-CC, RML-FNML, RML-Star, RML-LV) by the W3C Knowledge Graph Construction Community Group. Skolem IRI An IRI that replaces a blank node, conventionally under /.well-known/genid/. See RDF 1.1 Concepts §3.5. URI template A pattern such as /doc/{concept}/{id} that SPieGeL matches against incoming requests. Each template is bound to the queries that describe resources matching it.

docs.title: In scope
docs.text:
SPieGeL is a read-only Linked Data publishing server. It:

  • dereferences URIs according to a URI policy (id / doc / ns, plus Skolem IRIs and ELI paths);
  • assembles the description of a resource from one or more queries on one or more data sources;
  • serialises that description in the representation the client negotiates (HTML, Turtle, RDF/XML, N-Triples, JSON-LD), optionally per profile;
  • exposes a public, read-only SPARQL endpoint;
  • serves several data domains (tenants) from one stateless deployment;
  • enforces access levels on non-public data;
  • offers a portal over its domains, as a page of the umbrella domain's tenant;
  • ships command-line tools for writing and checking configuration (spiegel-tools).

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text:
• Writing data. SPieGeL never modifies a data source. Loading and transforming data (ETL) is a separate concern.
  • Managing vocabularies. Ontologies, concept schemes, SHACL shapes and catalogues are maintained elsewhere and loaded into the data sources. SPieGeL publishes them.
  • Serving event streams. Linked Data Event Streams publish the same resources and are served by an LDES server, such as OpenLDES's. SPieGeL makes them discoverable (ADR 0006).
  • Integrating data across domains. Consumers combine resources themselves, by dereferencing, by replicating event streams or with SPARQL (ADR 0006). The portal's federated SPARQL editor does so in the visitor's browser (ADR 0025).
  • Indexes across domains, such as labels or search terms gathered from several domains. They are stores of their own, filled by the loading chain; SPieGeL reads them like any data source (ADR 0026).
  • Other distributions of the data, such as OGC API Features or WFS layers and downloads. They carry the things' URIs, so that SPieGeL's subject pages serve as their landing pages (ADR 0007).
  • Edge concerns that belong to the reverse proxy, such as TLS termination, HSTS, generic request limits and flood protection. The 303, CORS and the real rate limits move into SPieGeL (ADR 0022).

docs.title: Phasing
docs.text: The requirements are prioritised with MoSCoW (see Traceability). The phases follow from that.

docs.title: Phase 1: basic service
docs.text:
Enough to publish a single public catalogue (for example a catalogue of simulation models) from a single SPARQL data source:

  • configurable data sources (SPARQL first);
  • configurable URI templates, each bound to its own query, with the 303 from id to doc;
  • descriptions bounded to their subject, with paging of large properties and a ceiling on their size;
  • content negotiation over the common RDF serialisations and HTML;
  • simple HTML subject pages that also carry their data as embedded JSON-LD;
  • a front page generated from the data it publishes (catalogues, thesauri, classes);
  • a dataset description and a findable licence per domain;
  • caching tied to the data version, and the response-time targets of Performance and availability;
  • rate limits per client, so that one client, such as a crawler, cannot take the data source's capacity from everyone else (ADR 0022).

No authentication is needed in this phase, because the catalogue is public.

docs.title: Phase 2: successor to the predecessor
docs.text:
Everything needed to switch off the predecessor:

  • several domains (tenants) in one deployment, each selected by host name;
  • the full URI policy, including ns pages, Skolem IRIs and ELI paths;
  • a public SPARQL endpoint compatible with the existing browser components;
  • content negotiation by profile;
  • context-specific HTML templates per URI template;
  • authentication (OIDC) and access levels.

docs.title: Later
docs.text:
