docs.text: Predecessor function Prez Where in the code /doc/{concept}/{id} as HTML and as RDF/XML, Turtle, N-Triples and JSON-LD RDF yes, plus annotated variants and GeoJSON. HTML no: it redirects to the separate Prez UI connegp_service.py, renderers/renderer.py Own composed query per concept and media type yes, in a different form: profiles per class, each with its own SHACL-defined content and its own media types. This is the closest match to what the predecessor intended reference_data/profiles, query_generation/shacl.py HTML view per concept outside Prez (Prez UI) — 303 from /id/ to /doc/ no. Resources live under CURIE paths (/catalogs/ex:abc/…) or at /object?iri=, not at their own IRI routers/base_router.py /ns/{model} no dedicated support; vocabularies are shown as catalogues or concept schemes — Several domains in one service no: one data store and one endpoint structure per instance (a documented limitation) config.py, docs/custom_endpoints.md /sparql as a filtered proxy with HTML results proxy yes, filter no, and off by default. No HTML results routers/sparql.py, repositories/remote_sparql.py Access levels through OIDC no. Only an optional fixed request header that must be present (required_header), meant for an API gateway middleware.py Keyword search yes, including full-text search on Fuseki and Lucene query_generation/search_*.py Reconciliation, Linked Data Fragments, dumps no — Incoming relations by profile: an sh:inversePath in the profile's shape query_generation/shacl.py Blank nodes in outgoing relations yes, to a configurable depth (shext:bNodeDepth) query_generation/shacl.py Front-end components that need a same-origin /sparql yes, when the SPARQL endpoint is enabled routers/sparql.py Skolem IRIs and ELI paths no: identifiers are CURIEs in a fixed path structure — Caching partly: labels, CURIEs and class lookups are cached in process. Responses are not cached, and no Cache-Control, ETag or Vary headers are set cache.py, services/annotations.py

docs.title: Points to note before using it in production
docs.text:
As with the other reviews, these are listed so that SPieGeL avoids them, not as criticism of a project that is actively maintained.

  1. Not every query goes through the syntax tree. Most queries are built with sparql-grammar, but a few are still assembled from text with values from the request. → SPieGeL: NFR-SEC-04, and use one query-building mechanism throughout.
  2. The SPARQL pass-through forwards the caller's headers. When enabled, /sparql passes the query and almost all incoming request headers (only Host and X-Request-ID are removed) to the store. As the README says, whether updates are refused is up to the store. → SPieGeL: NFR-SEC-01.
  3. Permissive CORS. Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is combined with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, once in a custom middleware and again through Starlette's CORSMiddleware (which then reflects the caller's origin). Prez has no logins, so the impact is small, but this must not be copied into a service that has them. → SPieGeL: NFR-OPEN-01.
  4. Management endpoints are public. GET /purge-tbox-cache empties the label cache for anyone, and /tbox-cache returns its whole content. → SPieGeL: NFR-SEC-08.
  5. Unbounded, per-process label cache. The annotation cache has no expiry and no size limit. It grows with every new IRI seen, is not invalidated when the data changes, and differs between replicas. → SPieGeL: NFR-OPS-03.
  6. No HTTP caching support. Representations are negotiated on Accept and Accept-Profile without a Vary header, and there is no ETag or Cache-Control. An unsupported media type falls back to the default instead of 406. → SPieGeL: NFR-SEC-03, FR-CN-05.
  7. Generated queries are hard to tune. Profiles are concise, but the CONSTRUCT built from a SHACL shape (unions of property paths, blank-node depth, annotation and link look-ups) is not written by anyone. Prez makes it visible with _mediatype=application/sparql-query, which helps, but a slow page needs a profile change rather than a query fix. The README also notes that the endpoint structure is limited to two or three levels because "the SHACL parsing is not completely recursive".
  8. /health does not check the store. It always answers {"status": "ok"}. → SPieGeL: NFR-OPS-04.

docs.title: What SPieGeL can learn from it
docs.text:
• The profile model, as data. Use prof:Profile and the altr-ext: vocabulary to declare which profiles exist, which classes they apply to, which media types they offer and which is the default per class. Read _profile and _mediatype as well as Accept-Profile and Accept. Answer with Link headers (rel="profile", rel="alternate") and offer an alt representation that lists them all. This is the most directly reusable result of the review, for FR-CN-02, FR-CN-03, FR-CN-04 and FR-RA-03.
  • Deterministic ranking. Rank the available representations explicitly: requested profile, class match, the class's default profile, requested media type, then the default media type. That makes negotiation testable (NFR-Q-02).
  • A typed query builder. Building queries as a syntax tree rather than as text is the structural answer to NFR-SEC-04. In Jena that means the ARQ syntax classes (Query, ElementGroup, ElementPathBlock) or ParameterizedSparqlString. Prez also shows the counter-lesson: one builder must be used everywhere, with no exceptions for "simple" queries.
  • Declarative descriptions, at least as an option. A SHACL shape with property paths and blank-node depth (FR-RA-04) is a compact way to say "what this profile contains". SPieGeL could offer it next to hand-written query files (FR-RA-02), generating queries for the simple cases and keeping files for the tuned ones. See open question 19.
  • Show the generated query. Returning the query for a resource on request (_mediatype=application/sparql-query) is a cheap, powerful diagnostic. In SPieGeL it belongs behind NFR-SEC-08.
  • Labelled responses. Adding labels and descriptions for every referenced IRI, partly from bundled copies of common vocabularies, lets a generic page show readable names without extra round trips (FR-HTML-01). SPieGeL can do this inside its HTML rendering, with a bounded cache.
  • Bounded counts. Reporting "more than 100" instead of an exact total keeps listings cheap on large datasets (NFR-OPS-02).
  • SKOS hierarchy endpoints. Top concepts and narrowers with child counts are exactly what an incremental tree view needs (FR-HTML-05).
  • Timeouts at both ends. Prez sets an HTTP client timeout and also passes a timeout parameter to the store (timeout= by default, configurable through SPARQL_TIMEOUT_PARAM_NAME), so the store stops working as well (NFR-OPS-02).
  • Observability without a full tracing stack. A correlation ID on every request (returned in X-Request-ID, with a separate client-supplied ID), JSON logs with typed attributes and units in the names (duration_ms), and the time spent waiting on downstream calls (NFR-OPS-05).
  • Testing set-up. An embedded store for unit tests, Testcontainers for tests against a real triple store, and the OGC conformance test suite for the Features API. All three have direct equivalents on the JVM.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
• As a replacement for the predecessor: no. Prez does not dereference IRIs at their own paths, does not serve HTML, serves one store per instance and has no access levels. Its URI structure (CURIEs in fixed path levels) conflicts with the Flemish URI standard.
  • For phase 1 (a single public catalogue): possible, but awkward. DCAT catalogues and SKOS schemes are what Prez is best at, and search and profiles come for free. However, it needs Prez UI for HTML and edge rewrites from /id/ and /doc/ paths to /object?iri=. That makes it a poorer stopgap than Trifid.
  • As a reference for SPieGeL: the most valuable of the three. Its implementation of Content Negotiation by Profile is complete and data-driven, and SPieGeL should follow it closely. The typed query builder, bounded counts, SKOS hierarchy endpoints and observability practices are also worth adopting. The SHACL-generated queries are an idea to weigh, not to copy wholesale.

docs.title: Trifid code review
docs.text:
Trifid (Zazuko) is the most mature and most widely used pure Linked Data front end in the comparison. It is on a different stack (TypeScript on Node.js), so adopting it was never likely. We read its source code to find out what it actually does, how much of the predecessor's behaviour it covers, and which of its ideas are worth taking into SPieGeL.

Version reviewed: upstream commit 370eb49 (1 October 2026), trifid and trifid-core 6.1.0. A pnpm monorepo of twelve packages, about 6,600 lines of TypeScript excluding tests. Built on Fastify 5, Handlebars, the RDF/JS libraries (@zazuko/env, sparql-http-client) and OpenTelemetry. Apache-2.0. Shipped as npm packages and as a Docker image that starts from an example configuration.

docs.title: Core: a configurable plug-in host
docs.text:
trifid-core contains no Linked Data logic at all. It reads one YAML or JSON5 configuration file with four sections (server, globals, template, plugins) and mounts each plug-in on Fastify routes (lib/plugins/apply.ts).

  • Plug-ins are factories that receive the server, a logger, the merged configuration (globals overlaid with the plug-in's own config), a render function for Handlebars templates and a query function for the configured SPARQL endpoints. They return a route handler. Each entry in plugins names a module and can restrict it to paths, methods and hosts (Fastify route constraints). An order field sets the mounting order.
  • The same module can be mounted several times under different names, each with its own paths and configuration. This is how a site gets several subject-page variants.
  • Configuration layering: extends pulls in other configuration files recursively. Values can be resolved with env:NAME, file:path (relative to the configuration file) and cwd:path. config/schema.json validates the structure.
  • Built-in plug-ins: static files, a Handlebars view, a fixed redirect, /healthz (always answers OK) and a plug-in that passes values to templates.
  • Cross-cutting concerns: compression (including Turtle, N-Triples and JSON-LD), CORS, cookies, Accept parsing, a subpath for serving under a prefix, Pino logging, and OpenTelemetry traces and metrics (otel.ts).

docs.title: Entity renderer: subject pages and content negotiation
docs.text:
@zazuko/trifid-entity-renderer is the part that dereferences IRIs. By default it is mounted on GET /* and does the following for each request (entity-renderer/index.ts):

  1. Rebuild the IRI from protocol, host, port and path, and drop the query string. If datasetBaseUrl is configured, swap the request origin for that base. This lets data with production IRIs be browsed on localhost or a test host. Several base URLs may be configured; they are tried in order.
  2. Check that the resource exists with resourceExistsQuery (default ASK { <{{iri}}> ?p ?o }), once per base URL until one matches. If none matches, it returns 404.
  3. Optional data-driven redirects (followRedirects): a SELECT on the W3C HTTP in RDF vocabulary (2006 and 2011 versions) finds a stored http:GetRequest for the IRI and answers with its http:responseCode and http:location. With enableSchemaUrlRedirect, a schema:URL of type xsd:anyURI on the resource sends HTML clients to that URL.
  4. Fetch the description with resourceGraphQuery (default DESCRIBE <{{iri}}>). If resourceNoSlash is set and the IRI ends in /, it is treated as a container: the subjects whose IRI starts with it are listed through a FILTER REGEX.
  5. Negotiate the format (lib/headers.ts): ?format=ttl|jsonld|xml|nt|trig|csv|html overrides Accept. Otherwise mimeparse picks the best of JSON-LD, N-Triples, RDF/XML, Turtle, TriG, CSV and HTML.
  6. Machine formats are serialised from the parsed quad stream. CSV is a flattened key/value view of the JSON-LD.
  7. HTML goes through a server-side rendered Lit web component (@zazuko/rdf-entity-webcomponent with @lit-labs/ssr). A label loader first fetches labels for referenced IRIs that have none in the description: in chunks of 30, two at a time, with a timeout and a cap of 1,000 terms. The page also embeds the description as JSON-LD and shows a count of triples per named graph. Callers can change the rendering through query parameters: compactMode, technicalCues, embedNamedNodes, embedBlankNodes, maxLevel, lang and others.

All queries and the template (path) are configuration. Every query goes to the default endpoint in globals.endpoints. In the shipped configurations that is /query, so the entity renderer queries its own SPARQL proxy over HTTP.

docs.title: SPARQL proxy
docs.text:
@zazuko/trifid-plugin-sparql-proxy (sparql-proxy/index.ts) mounts /query for GET and POST.

  • It forwards the query as-is, as a POST form field, to the configured endpoint, adding basic-auth credentials or extra headers from the configuration. The response is streamed back with its status and content type, plus a Server-Timing header.
  • IRI rewriting: when rewrite is on, the instance's origin is replaced by datasetBaseUrl in the query text, and the other way round in the response stream (lib/ReplaceStream.ts). Callers can toggle this with ?rewrite=true|false (allowRewriteToggle, on by default).
  • Several named endpoints can be configured. The caller picks one with ?endpoint=name, which is then remembered in a cookie for 30 days.
  • A GET without parameters returns a SPARQL Service Description. A worker thread fetches it from the upstream endpoint at start-up and filters it to the sd: vocabulary. If that fails, a minimal one is generated.

docs.title: Other packages
docs.text: Package What it does trifid The ready-to-run server, plus example configurations (docker-sparql, docker-fetch, tbbt). trifid-handler-fetch Loads an RDF file (local or remote) into an in-memory Oxigraph store in a worker thread and serves SPARQL on it, with a 30-second timeout per query. Useful for demonstrations and small datasets. trifid-plugin-yasgui YASGUI query editor at /sparql, with two extra result views: a Leaflet map for geo:wktLiteral values and a pivot table. trifid-plugin-graph-explorer Zazuko's Graph Explorer (visual browsing), with SPARQL dialect presets. trifid-plugin-spex SPEX, a schema and data explorer. trifid-plugin-i18n Interface translations; the chosen language is kept in a cookie. trifid-markdown-content Serves directories of Markdown files as multilingual HTML pages. trifid-plugin-ckan DCAT-AP-CH export for the opendata.swiss CKAN harvester. trifid-plugin-iiif IIIF manifests; marked as no longer used.

docs.title: Coverage of the predecessor's functions
docs.text: Predecessor function Trifid Where in the code /doc/{concept}/{id} as HTML and as RDF/XML, Turtle, N-Triples and JSON-LD yes, plus TriG and CSV; override with ?format= entity-renderer/lib/headers.ts, core/lib/sparql.ts Own composed query per concept and media type partly: one existence query and one description query per entity-renderer instance. Mounting one instance per path pattern gives each concept its own query, but not several queries per concept, and not different queries per media type entity-renderer/lib/config.ts, core/lib/plugins/apply.ts HTML view per concept yes, through the instance's path template, but the description itself is always rendered by the generic web component entity-renderer/index.ts 303 from /id/ to /doc/ not as a rule. The redirect plug-in has one fixed target. Redirects can be stored in the data per IRI (HTTP in RDF), which does not scale to a whole URI pattern core/plugins/redirect.ts, redirectQuery /ns/{model} yes, as a separate entity-renderer instance on that path — Several domains in one service partly. Plug-ins can be bound to host names, but the entity renderer and the label loader always query the single default endpoint, and its relative URL is resolved against the listener address rather than the request's host. In practice: one instance per domain core/lib/sparql.ts (initQuery), core/index.ts /sparql as a filtered proxy with HTML results proxy yes, filter no. Every query is passed through unchanged; read-only behaviour depends entirely on the store's credentials. HTML results through YASGUI sparql-proxy/index.ts, yasgui Access levels through OIDC no. No user authentication at all; the named endpoints are selectable by any caller sparql-proxy/index.ts (?endpoint=) Keyword search, reconciliation, Linked Data Fragments, dumps no — Incoming relations no, unless the store's DESCRIBE includes them or resourceGraphQuery is replaced entity-renderer/lib/config.ts Blank nodes in outgoing relations depends on the store's DESCRIBE; the renderer embeds whatever blank nodes it receives renderer/entity.ts (embedBlankNodes) Front-end components that need a same-origin /sparql yes: the proxy on /query (or another path) is same-origin sparql-proxy Skolem IRIs and ELI paths yes, generically: any path under the base URL is dereferenced if it exists in the data entity-renderer/index.ts Caching no: every request goes to the store, and no Cache-Control, ETag or Vary headers are set —

docs.title: Points to note before using it in production
docs.text:
As with the LodView review, these are properties of the design that matter on a public network. They are listed so that SPieGeL avoids them, not as criticism of a well-maintained project.

  1. Unfiltered SPARQL pass-through. The proxy forwards any query text, with the configured credentials, and sets no timeout of its own on the upstream call. Protection against expensive queries and updates sits entirely with the store. → SPieGeL: NFR-SEC-01, NFR-OPS-02.
  2. Endpoints are chosen by the caller. ?endpoint= and the endpointName cookie select any configured endpoint. So endpoints cannot be used to separate public from protected data. → SPieGeL: FR-AC-03, NFR-SEC-02.
  3. Browser-side credentials for SPEX. If user and password are configured for the SPEX plug-in, they are serialised into the HTML page for every visitor (spex/index.ts, views/index.hbs).
  4. Permissive CORS. CORS is registered with origin: true and credentials: true, which reflects any origin and allows credentials. Trifid has no logins, so the impact is small, but this setting must not be copied into a service that has them. → SPieGeL: NFR-OPEN-01.
  5. Queries built by string substitution. {{iri}} is replaced textually (replaceIriInQuery). The IRI is rebuilt through the WHATWG URL class, which percent-encodes <, >, " and spaces in paths, and we found no way to break out of <…>. That safety comes from URL normalisation, though, not from the query layer. In the container query the IRI ends up unescaped inside a regular expression, so regex metacharacters in a path change what matches. → SPieGeL: NFR-SEC-04.
  6. No Vary: Accept and no 406. HTML and RDF are served from the same URL without Vary: Accept, so a shared cache can return the wrong format. An unsupported Accept value falls back to HTML instead of 406. → SPieGeL: FR-CN-05, NFR-SEC-03.
  7. Cost per page. An HTML page takes at least an ASK (one per configured base URL until a match), a DESCRIBE, optionally a redirect SELECT, and up to 34 label queries (1,000 terms in chunks of 30). All go over HTTP through the instance's own proxy, and none are cached. The container query (FILTER REGEX(STR(?s), "^…")) scans every typed subject.
  8. Rewriting is plain text substitution. The base URL is also replaced inside literals and in query text. ReplaceStream keeps everything after the last match in memory, so a large response that contains no match is buffered whole before it is sent. Its final flush also builds a regular expression from the base URL without escaping it.
  9. /healthz does not check anything. It always answers OK, whatever the state of the store. → SPieGeL: NFR-OPS-04.
  10. The description depends on the store. With the default DESCRIBE, what a subject page shows (blank nodes, incoming triples) differs between Fuseki, Virtuoso, Stardog and GraphDB. → SPieGeL keeps the description in its own queries (FR-RA-01, FR-RA-04).

docs.title: What SPieGeL can learn from it
docs.text:
These are the ideas worth taking over, with where they apply.

  • Base-URL rewriting for non-production environments. Being able to browse and query data with production IRIs on a test or local host is useful for SPieGeL's own test and acceptance environments. SPieGeL should do it at the term level (rewriting IRIs in the parsed result and binding IRIs in the query) rather than with text substitution. Relates to FR-URI-01 and NFR-OPS-06.
  • Batched label lookup with limits. Fetching labels for referenced IRIs in chunks, with bounded concurrency, a timeout and a cap on the number of terms, is a good pattern for readable subject pages that cannot overload the store. It is a concrete form of NFR-OPS-02 for FR-HTML-01.
  • Redirects as data. Recording moved or retired URIs in the store with the W3C HTTP vocabulary lets data owners manage them without a deployment. That supports NFR-OPEN-02 (stable URIs). See open question 18.
  • Mount the same handler several times. One generic subject-page handler with configuration per path pattern (queries and template) is close to SPieGeL's URI-template model (FR-URI-01, FR-RA-01, FR-HTML-03). SPieGeL adds what Trifid lacks: several queries per template, conditions on type and profile (FR-RA-03), and a tenant boundary (FR-MT-01).
  • Layered, file-based configuration. extends together with env: and file: resolvers gives a shared base configuration with small overlays per environment or tenant. It fits NFR-OPS-06 and the "queries as files" approach of FR-RA-02.
  • Format override with short names. ?format=ttl|jsonld|xml|nt|html is a compact, linkable form of FR-CN-02.
  • Service Description on the SPARQL endpoint. Answering a bare GET with an sd:Service description is cheap and helps clients. A candidate addition to FR-SPARQL-01.
  • Observability. OpenTelemetry metrics per endpoint and format (sparql_entities_dereferenced_total, sparql_queries_total) and a Server-Timing header on proxied queries are good examples for NFR-OPS-05.
  • Useful extras on the query page. A map view for geo:wktLiteral results and a pivot table are cheap features that suit spatial data. They are relevant to FR-SPARQL-03.
  • An in-memory store for demonstrations. Serving a file through an embedded store (Oxigraph there; Jena's in-memory dataset for SPieGeL) makes a self-contained demonstration and test set-up easy.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
• As a replacement for the predecessor: no. Like LodView, it lacks access levels, a filtered SPARQL endpoint, search, several queries per concept and real multi-tenancy. On top of that it is outside the team's stack.
  • For phase 1 (a single public catalogue): yes, functionally. One catalogue, one public store, content negotiation, subject pages, a SPARQL proxy and YASGUI are what Trifid does out of the box, and it is actively maintained. If a stopgap were needed, Trifid would be a better one than LodView, provided the store enforces read-only access and query limits, and the reverse proxy adds the 303, caching and Vary.
  • As a reference for SPieGeL: valuable in its ideas, not in its code. The plug-in host is a clean, small design, and the points under What SPieGeL can learn from it are proven in production. Its weak spots (text-substituted queries and rewriting, no caching, endpoints chosen by the caller) are exactly the areas where SPieGeL's requirements are stricter.

docs.title: Reference: the UniProt SPARQL service
docs.text: UniProt is not a tool to reuse, but a public SPARQL service that does several things SPieGeL needs, at a scale far beyond the department's domains: 244 billion triples in release 2026_03, served by QLever (a candidate store, see open question 29). We looked at https://sparql.uniprot.org/ on 7 October 2026. Its response times are on Performance and availability.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Example queries are the home page. The page is mainly a list of example queries, each with a one-line description in plain language. A click opens the query in the editor, through a URL that carries the query (/sparql/?query=…).
  • Example queries are data. Each example is a SHACL sh:SPARQLExecutable with the query text, an rdfs:comment and keywords. The examples are loaded into the endpoint itself, so they can be queried like any other data, and are published under /.well-known/sparql-examples/. This follows the convention of the SIB SPARQL examples, shared by several life-science services.
  • The endpoint describes itself. GET /sparql with Accept: text/turtle returns a SPARQL 1.1 Service Description of 474 kB: the result formats, features such as the union default graph and federated queries, the data version (pav:version "2026_03") and its release date, and all 21 named graphs. Per named graph it adds VoID statistics: the number of triples, distinct subjects and objects, and class and property partitions. A client, or a person, can see what the data contains without running a single query. /.well-known/void itself answers with an empty body.
  • The same facts are readable on the page. An About block gives the number of triples in this release, the release, the query timeout (45 minutes), that the default graph is the union of all graphs, and the number of named graphs. It links to the vocabulary, a tutorial, and statistics with diagrams. The licence (CC BY 4.0) is in the footer of every page.
  • Responses are versioned by release. Responses carry ETag: W/"2026_03", Cache-Control: public and an Expires one day later, so caches can keep them until the data changes.
  • Withdrawn entries stay available. An obsolete named graph keeps entries that are no longer current.
  • The editor helps with prefixes. Next to Clear and Submit, an Add common prefixes button inserts the usual PREFIX lines. The editor is YASQE.

docs.title: How it is built
docs.text:
UniProt has two separate front ends, built in opposite ways.

  • The SPARQL page (sparql.uniprot.org) is plain XHTML, rendered on the server by SIB's Java web application behind Apache. Query results also come back as a server-rendered HTML table. In the browser there are two style sheets, the YASQE editor (YASGUI 2.11) from a CDN, and one small script without a framework (sparql.js) for the prefix and clear buttons. That script reads the prefixes from the endpoint itself, as SHACL sh:prefix and sh:namespace declarations, the same convention as the examples: prefixes are data too. This is the approach SPieGeL takes: content rendered on the server, JavaScript only for the editor (NFR-UI-04).
  • The main site (www.uniprot.org) is a client-side application. Its HTML holds only an empty <div id="root">. Its public code (MIT) uses React 19 with TypeScript, React Router and webpack, with separate bundles for modern and older browsers, and its own design system (franklin-sites). The protein visualisations are web components (Nightingale and ProtVista, built with Lit), wrapped for React. Its data comes from a REST API (rest.uniprot.org), not from SPARQL. Like data.vlaanderen.be, it shows nothing without JavaScript.

SIB also publishes a newer editor, @sib-swiss/sparql-editor (MIT, last change August 2026). It is a web component built on YASGUI. It takes autocompletion for classes and properties from the endpoint's VoID description, filtered by the class of the subject at the cursor, the example queries from their SHACL descriptions, and the prefixes from sh:prefix. It needs no configuration beyond that metadata, so it works on any store whose endpoint publishes it. SPieGeL publishes exactly that metadata (FR-META-03, FR-HTML-15, FR-SPARQL-04), which makes the component a candidate for SPieGeL's SPARQL editor (open question 37).

docs.title: What SPieGeL takes from it
docs.text:
UniProt SPieGeL Example queries as SHACL in git and in the endpoint, at /.well-known/sparql-examples/ FR-SPARQL-04 Service Description with VoID statistics per named graph FR-META-03, FR-META-01, FR-HTML-15 Key facts (size, version, timeout, graphs, licence) readable on the page FR-META-01, FR-META-02 Entity tag per data release NFR-OPS-03, Performance and availability Withdrawn entries still described FR-URI-09 A URL per query; common prefixes in the editor, read from sh:prefix declarations FR-SPARQL-03 Content rendered on the server, JavaScript only for the editor NFR-UI-04 An editor that autocompletes from VoID and lists the SHACL examples (@sib-swiss/sparql-editor) FR-SPARQL-03, open question 37

What SPieGeL does not copy is the 45-minute timeout for anonymous queries. UniProt's store and hardware can afford it; SPieGeL keeps a configured timeout per tenant (NFR-PERF-03, NFR-OPS-02).

Example queries as data also serve a purpose beyond the editor: a set of questions in plain language with their correct SPARQL is ready-made context for applications that translate questions into queries (open question 34).

docs.title: Hexagonal design
docs.text:
SPieGeL uses a hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters). The domain core holds the rules that the predecessor spreads over scripts, templates and an XML catalogue. These rules include which URI template matches, which queries describe a resource, which profile applies, and which access level a caller has. The core depends only on interfaces (ports). Everything technology-specific lives in adapters.

Status

This is the design as proposed by the analysis. Choices that need a formal decision will be recorded as ADRs.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
SPieGeL reads RDF from data sources, which are SPARQL endpoints (FR-DS-01). Whether it may also read a file such as HDT in-process is open question 29. A triple store holds RDF that is loaded into it, including RDF that the loading chain has materialised from non-RDF sources with RML. A relational source that must be current is translated per request by Ontop, which offers its own SPARQL endpoint, so SPieGeL reads it like a store (ADR 0009).

flowchart LR
    CL[Clients and browsers] --> PX[Reverse proxy] --> S[SPieGeL]
    S -->|SPARQL| TS[(Triple store)]
    S -->|SPARQL| OT[Ontop endpoint]
    OT -->|R2RML, SQL per query| RDB[(PostgreSQL, Trino)]
    S -->|SPARQL| CX[(Cross-domain index, if any)]
    S --> IDP[OIDC provider]
    S -.->|Link rel=collection| LDES[LDES server]
    subgraph cfg [Configuration, outside SPieGeL]
        REPO[Configuration repository] -->|CI with spiegel-tools| ART[Configuration artefact]
    end
    ART --> S
    subgraph lc [Loading chain, outside SPieGeL]
        SRC[CSV, JSON, XML, Web APIs, periodic relational extracts] --> RML[RML processor]
    end
    RML -->|materialised RDF| TS
    RML -->|labels, search terms| CX

The portal and its federated SPARQL editor are pages of the umbrella domain's tenant, not separate services; the editor's queries run in the visitor's browser (ADR 0025). An index of data from several domains, such as labels or search terms, is never held by SPieGeL: it is a store of its own, filled by the loading chain, and read like any data source. Tools for writing and checking configuration are a separate artefact, spiegel-tools (ADR 0026).

docs.title: Ports and adapters
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph inbound [Inbound adapters]
        WEB[HTTP: /id /doc /ns /eli /.well-known/genid]
        SPQ[HTTP: /sparql]
        SRCH[HTTP: /keywordsearch]
    end
    subgraph core [Domain core]
        UC1([DereferenceResource])
        UC2([RunSparqlQuery: guarded pass-through])
        UC3([Search])
        M[UriTemplate · ResourceType · QuerySpec · Profile · AccessLevel · Tenant]
    end
    subgraph outbound [Outbound adapters]
        CFG[Tenant configuration]
        IDP[Identity: token → AccessLevel]
        REN[Renderers: RDF formats, HTML]
        CACHE[Cache]
        DS[(SPARQL data source: triple store or Ontop)]
        SI[Search: the store's full-text index]
    end
    WEB --> UC1
    SPQ --> UC2
    SRCH --> UC3
    inbound -.-> CFG
    inbound -.-> IDP
    inbound -.-> REN
    UC1 --> CACHE
    UC1 --> DS
    UC2 --> DS
    UC3 --> SI

Solid arrows are calls from a use case. Dotted arrows are calls that an inbound adapter makes through a port of the core, before or after the use case: it resolves the tenant and the caller's access level first, and renders the result last (see Request flow). These ports are defined in the core so that the web adapter does not depend on the HTML or security adapter. The use cases receive the tenant and the access level as input; they do not call the identity provider themselves.

The order in which these parts act on a request is described in Request flow.

docs.title: Domain core
docs.text:
Concept Responsibility Tenant A domain: host names, data sources (one of them named for /sparql), licence, language priority, URI templates, profiles, HTML theme. Read from Turtle by the configuration adapter; the core never sees Turtle (ADR 0012). DataSource A named SPARQL endpoint for one access level, with a key to its credentials and a declaration whether it enforces graph permissions (ADR 0011). UriTemplate A path pattern with variables typed by a pattern, and the ResourceType it identifies. Also models the id → doc relation and the 303. A tenant normally has one generic template for every concept, plus optional, more specific templates for exceptions (ADR 0012). ResourceType What kind of resource a template yields, and which QuerySpecs describe it. QuerySpec A query (stored as data), the data source it runs on, and the conditions (profile, media type) under which it runs. Replaces the predecessor's XML query catalogue. Profile A named view of a resource (for example summary or full), negotiated per Content Negotiation by Profile. AccessLevel An ordered type (public < internal < confidential < secret < top secret). The caller's level is the highest level among their roles. ResourceDescription The merged RDF result, independent of format: a Jena Graph (ADR 0010). QueryPolicy What a query may do: the allowed query forms, and no SERVICE. Applied to every query on /sparql and to every tenant query when the configuration is loaded. It names no graphs; the store decides what a level sees (ADR 0011).

Use cases (inbound ports):

  • DereferenceResource: given a tenant, a path, the negotiated media type and profile, and the caller's access level, return a ResourceDescription, a redirect (303 from id to doc, or 301 for a moved resource), a tombstone (410), or "not found".
  • RunSparqlQuery: run a read-only query for a tenant at the caller's access level, on the one data source the tenant names for /sparql. This is a guarded pass-through rather than domain logic: the core does not interpret the query, but checks it against the QueryPolicy through the QueryInspector port, and applies the access level, the bounded pool, the timeout and the result limit.
  • Search: keyword search for a tenant at the caller's access level.

Outbound ports:

Port Adapters DataSourcePort SPARQL over HTTP (Jena), for triple stores and for Ontop endpoints over relational sources (ADR 0009) QueryInspector Checks query text against a QueryPolicy: strict SPARQL 1.1 parsing and a walk over the syntax tree, in spiegel-adapter-sparql (ADR 0011) SearchPort The data source's own full-text index through SPARQL, such as bif:contains or ql:contains-word (FR-SRCH-01) TenantConfigurationPort Turtle in SPieGeL's configuration vocabulary, validated with SHACL, with .rq files for queries (ADR 0012). Delivered as a versioned artefact, mounted read-only (ADR 0013) CachePort In-memory; later a shared cache IdentityPort OIDC through Spring Security RateLimitPort In memory per node, each counting up to its share of the limit; later a shared store, falling back to the count per node when it fails (ADR 0022) RendererPort Jena RIOT for RDF formats; a template engine for HTML

docs.title: Mapping from the predecessor
docs.text: Predecessor concept SPieGeL equivalent Note Java accessor Adapter (inbound or outbound) Usually a direct translation Scripts for /doc, /ns, /sparql and search Use cases in the core Currently mix caching, security and domain logic; to be separated Routes generated at runtime per domain One set of controllers with Tenant resolved from the host name No per-domain code XML query catalogue and query templates ResourceType + QuerySpec + Profile The most hidden business logic of the predecessor. Now typed and tested RDF serialisation Renderer adapter (Jena RIOT) — XSLT HTML rendering HTML renderer adapter Template engine to be decided File-based second-level cache CachePort The key includes the access level and profile (NFR-SEC-03) OIDC flow scripts Spring Security OAuth2 resource server / client Large simplification Environment variables → configuration @ConfigurationProperties + tenant configuration files — Concurrency throttle Bounded executor or bulkhead per data source NFR-OPS-02

docs.title: Rules that keep the core clean
docs.text:
• The core has no dependency on Spring, servlet APIs, Jena's HTTP client or any template engine. It uses Jena's graph types (Graph, Node, Triple from jena-core), so that descriptions can be merged without conversion, but nothing from jena-arq: it neither parses nor runs SPARQL, nor reads or writes RDF formats (ADR 0010).
  • Adapters depend on the core; the core never depends on adapters.
  • Authorisation is part of the use case, not of a filter that can be bypassed by a cache hit (NFR-SEC-03).

docs.title: Module structure
docs.text:
The proposed Maven module layout follows the hexagonal design. Each adapter is its own module, so that its dependencies cannot leak into the core.

spiegel/                         (parent POM, packaging pom)
├── spiegel-core                 domain model, use cases, ports. No Spring.
├── spiegel-adapter-sparql       DataSourcePort over SPARQL 1.1 (Apache Jena)
├── spiegel-adapter-web          HTTP inbound: dereferencing, 303, content negotiation, /sparql
├── spiegel-adapter-html         RendererPort for HTML (template engine, Flux design system, front-end build)
├── spiegel-adapter-security     IdentityPort: OIDC, roles → AccessLevel
├── spiegel-adapter-config       TenantConfigurationPort: Turtle + .rq files, SHACL validation (jena-shacl)
├── spiegel-app                  Spring Boot application: wiring, caching, health, packaging
└── spiegel-tools                command-line tools for configuration and CI: context generator,
                                 vocabulary extractor, configuration validator

docs.title: Dependency rules
docs.text:
flowchart BT
    core[spiegel-core]
    sparql[spiegel-adapter-sparql] --> core
    web[spiegel-adapter-web] --> core
    html[spiegel-adapter-html] --> core
    sec[spiegel-adapter-security] --> core
    cfg[spiegel-adapter-config] --> core
    app[spiegel-app] --> sparql & web & html & sec & cfg
    tools[spiegel-tools] --> core & cfg
  • spiegel-core depends on nothing in this project, and only on a minimal set of libraries.
  • Adapters depend on spiegel-core only, never on each other.
  • spiegel-tools is not part of the server. It reuses the configuration model and validation of spiegel-adapter-config, so that CI and the server check the same rules, and is delivered as a command-line tool (ADR 0026).
  • Only spiegel-app knows all modules. It is the only module that depends on Spring Boot's auto-configuration.
  • These rules are enforced by a test (for example with ArchUnit), not only by convention.

docs.title: Why this split
docs.text:
The modules are a direct consequence of the hexagonal design: one module for the core, one per adapter, and one that assembles them. Separate Maven modules, rather than packages in one module, are chosen for these reasons:

  1. The compiler guards the boundaries. A module can only use what its own POM declares. Jena's HTTP client is only in spiegel-adapter-sparql, Jena's serialisers (RIOT) only in the adapters that render RDF, and Spring MVC only in spiegel-adapter-web. The core cannot import a Spring or Jena HTTP class by accident, because it would not compile. With packages in one module, such a boundary is only a convention.
  2. A test guards what the compiler cannot see. ArchitectureTest (ArchUnit) checks on every build that the core stays free of frameworks and that adapters do not depend on each other.
  3. Adapters can be replaced. A second store type is a second implementation of the same DataSourcePort, without any change to the core. A relational source needs not even that: Ontop offers a SPARQL endpoint, so spiegel-adapter-sparql reads it (ADR 0009). The same holds for the template engine, which is still to be chosen (open question 9).
  4. The core can be tested without infrastructure. The rules for URI templates, profiles, access levels and merging descriptions are tested without a server, a store or a browser (NFR-Q-01, NFR-Q-02).
  5. Each technology stays in its own module. This matters especially for spiegel-adapter-html, which gets a front-end build (Node.js, pnpm, Flux; see Design system: Flux) that must not leak into the rest of the build.
  6. Modules arrive by phase. Phase 1 needs no authentication, so spiegel-adapter-security arrives in phase 2 (ADR 0004: modules are added when they are needed).
  7. It prevents what the predecessor shows. There, caching, security and domain logic are mixed in scripts, and the query catalogue lives outside any type system or test (see Mapping from the predecessor). Module boundaries keep these concerns apart.

The split has costs: - More build files. There are more POMs and some boilerplate. - Some concerns cross modules. The cache lives in spiegel-app but must follow the core's rules (NFR-SEC-03), and logging must be consistent in every module. - The core depends on jena-core. It uses Jena's graph types to merge descriptions without conversion, but nothing from jena-arq, so it has no SPARQL engine, HTTP client or serialisers (ADR 0010). ArchitectureTest enforces this.

docs.title: Phase 1 subset
docs.text: Phase 1 (see Scope) needs spiegel-core, spiegel-adapter-sparql, spiegel-adapter-web, spiegel-adapter-html, spiegel-adapter-config and spiegel-app. spiegel-adapter-security arrives in phase 2. spiegel-tools arrives with its first tool, such as the context generator of ADR 0017.

docs.title: Group and artefact identifiers
docs.text: Decided in ADR 0004: group be.vlaanderen.omgeving.spiegel, artefacts as listed above, with spiegel-parent as the parent POM.

docs.title: Request flow
docs.text:
This chapter follows a request through SPieGeL, from arrival to response. It complements the hexagonal design, which lists the parts, by fixing the order in which they act. For each step it says which part acts and which requirements it covers. The predecessor's flow is described in Request flows.

Status

This is the flow as proposed by the analysis. Steps that depend on an open choice say so and link to the open questions. Steps marked phase 2 do not exist in phase 1, where every caller is unauthenticated and so has the public access level (see Scope).

docs.title: Principles behind the order
docs.text:
1. Cheap decisions first. Tenant, URI template, 303 and content negotiation need no data, so they come before any query.
  2. Authorise before the cache. The caller's access level is known before the cache is consulted, and it is part of the cache key (NFR-SEC-03).
  3. Data before format. The core produces a format-independent ResourceDescription. Media type and HTML presentation are applied after the cache, so one cached description serves every format of the same profile.
  4. Fail closed. A resource that does not exist and one the caller may not see give the same answer (NFR-SEC-07). A description with a failed query is never cached or served. One cut off at the ceiling says so (NFR-OPS-09).

docs.title: Dereferencing a resource: /id, /doc, /ns, Skolem IRIs and ELI
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant P as Reverse proxy
    participant W as Web adapter
    participant T as Tenant configuration
    participant I as Identity adapter
    participant U as DereferenceResource (core)
    participant K as Cache
    participant D as Data source
    participant R as Renderer
    C->>P: GET https://{host}/doc/{concept}/{id}
    Note over P: TLS, HSTS, X-Forwarded-*<br/>flood protection per address
    P->>W: GET /doc/{concept}/{id} (Accept, Accept-Profile)
    W->>T: tenant for host name
    W->>I: caller → access level (phase 2)
    W->>W: rate limit per client, tenant and kind (429)
    W->>W: match URI template
    alt id template
        W-->>P: 303 See Other → doc URI
        P-->>C: 303
    end
    W->>W: negotiate media type and profile
    W->>U: tenant, template match, profile, access level
    U->>K: lookup (tenant, IRI, profile, access level)
    alt cache miss
        U->>D: run the profile's queries (access level's credentials)
        D-->>U: RDF
        U->>U: merge, check completeness
        U->>K: store
    end
    U-->>W: ResourceDescription or not found
    W->>R: render (media type, profile, presentation rules)
    R-->>W: body
    W-->>P: 200 with Vary, Link, Content-Location, ETag, CORS, CSP
    P-->>C: 200

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
# Step Part Requirements 0 Edge. The reverse proxy terminates TLS, adds HSTS and passes the original host, scheme and client address in X-Forwarded-* headers. SPieGeL trusts those headers only from the proxy's configured addresses. The proxy also sets generic limits (sizes, connections, time-outs) and protects against floods with a generous limit per address. It does not filter on content, answer the 303 or set CORS headers: SPieGeL does (ADR 0022). reverse proxy NFR-OPS-08 1 Receive. Assign a request identifier, start timing, and log in a structured format, without personal data from the request (NFR-PRIV-02). web adapter NFR-OPS-05, NFR-PRIV-02 2 Resolve the tenant from the host name. An unknown host gets 404. web adapter, TenantConfigurationPort FR-MT-01, FR-MT-02 3 Identify the caller (phase 2). A bearer token (OpenID Connect or client credentials) is validated on every request, with no server-side session. A caller without a token is an unauthenticated client and gets the public level, the lowest. In phase 1 every caller is one. The level is the highest one granted by the caller's roles. web adapter, IdentityPort FR-AC-01, FR-AC-02, NFR-OPS-01 3a Check the rate limit for this client, tenant and kind of request, through RateLimitPort. Over the limit gives 429 with Retry-After (step E7). No query has been run yet. A limit per authenticated client can only be applied after step 3. In phase 1 each node counts up to its share of the limit (ADR 0022). web adapter → RateLimitPort NFR-OPS-08 4 Match the URI template. When several match, the most specific wins: more literal characters, then more variables. Variables are typed by a pattern, so an invalid value gives 404 (no match) without a query, not an error. No match gives 404. A value that matches is not checked against a list: the data decides whether the resource exists (step 12), and a negative result is cached per data version (ADR 0012). core (UriTemplate) FR-URI-01, FR-URI-03 to 05 5 id → doc. If the template is an id template, answer 303 See Other with the matching doc URI in Location, for every media type. The data is not consulted, so the redirect reveals nothing about whether the resource exists or is visible. core (UriTemplate), web adapter FR-URI-02, NFR-SEC-07 6 Negotiate the media type. A format suffix or _format overrides Accept. Otherwise the client's quality values are weighed against SPieGeL's quality per format; no Accept, or only */*, gives HTML. Nothing acceptable gives 406. web adapter FR-CN-01, FR-CN-02, FR-CN-05, FR-CN-08 7 Negotiate the profile. _profile overrides Accept-Profile. If nothing is asked for, or the request cannot be met, the resource type's default profile for this media type applies, for example a lighter HTML profile. The response says which profile was used. core (Profile) FR-CN-03 7a Choose the language for HTML: ?lang=, then Accept-Language, then the tenant's default, among the languages the tenant offers. It affects rendering only, not the queries or the cache. web adapter FR-HTML-12 8 Call the use case DereferenceResource with the tenant, the template match (resource IRI and type), the profile and the access level. web adapter → core — 9 Select the queries. Those QuerySpecs of the resource type whose conditions hold for the profile. The conditions are typed and tested. core (ResourceType, QuerySpec) FR-RA-01 to 03 10 Look up the cache under (tenant, resource IRI, profile, access level). The media type is not part of the key, because the cache holds RDF: a read-only description that every format of the profile is serialised from (ADR 0020). core → CachePort NFR-SEC-03, NFR-OPS-03 11 Run the queries on a miss, on each query's named data source, with the credentials for the caller's access level. The resource IRI is bound as a term, not pasted into text. Queries run concurrently, within a bounded pool per data source and with a timeout. core → DataSourcePort FR-DS-01, FR-AC-03, NFR-SEC-02, NFR-SEC-04, NFR-OPS-02 12 Merge and check. Merge the results into one ResourceDescription, with blank nodes to the configured depth and owl:unionOf lists expanded for vocabularies. If a query failed or timed out, the request fails (step E2), and nothing is cached. A description that reaches the tenant's ceiling on triples is not a failure: it is served and cached, marked as incomplete in the RDF and in a header (NFR-OPS-09). If the description is empty, SPieGeL looks for a recorded move or removal of this URI: a move gives 301 to the new URI, a removal gives 410 with its tombstone (FR-URI-08, FR-URI-10, FR-URI-11). Otherwise the result is not found: the resource does not exist, or the caller may not see it. Otherwise, add the links between the document and the thing it describes (foaf:primaryTopic, foaf:page). core FR-RA-01, FR-RA-04, FR-RA-05, FR-URI-06 to 08, FR-URI-10, FR-URI-11, NFR-OPS-09, NFR-SEC-07 13 Store a complete description in the cache, under the tenant's current data version, configuration version and SPieGeL version. It stays valid until one of them changes, usually because the loading chain signals a new data version; the tenant's fixed lifetime is only a fallback. core → CachePort NFR-OPS-03 14 Render. For RDF formats, serialise with Jena RIOT, streaming where possible. For HTML, see Rendering HTML. RendererPort FR-CN-01, FR-HTML-01 15 Set the headers and send the response. See Response headers. A HEAD request gets the same status and headers, without the body. web adapter FR-CN-04, FR-CN-09, NFR-OPEN-01, NFR-UI-03 16 Log and measure: status, duration, and cache hit or miss, per tenant and data source. web adapter NFR-OPS-05

A conditional request (If-None-Match) whose ETag still matches gets 304 Not Modified after step 13, without rendering. The tag is computed from versions and the negotiated variant alone.

docs.title: Rendering HTML
docs.text:
HTML is rendered from the same ResourceDescription, after the cache. The steps are:

  1. Labels. Labels of the properties and of the linked resources, and their types, must be present, because every IRI on the page becomes a link labelled with its label (FR-HTML-10). Labels from the domain come from a query that the HTML profile declares for that purpose, not from whatever the main queries happen to return (see Data-dependent HTML rendering). That query is one of the profile's QuerySpecs: the core runs it in step 11, at the caller's access level, and caches its result with the description. Terms without a label in the domain's data get one from the index of vocabulary extracts that SPieGeL builds at start-up from the configuration (FR-HTML-11, ADR 0021), with no query. The renderer itself queries nothing.
  2. Presentation rules. The tenant's rules, combined with the shared defaults, choose the presentation blocks and components: by type, by predicate, by the predicate's own type and by datatype. → FR-HTML-06. How the rules are expressed is open question 21.
  3. Geometries. WKT literals are written into the page as they are, with their CRS (the GeoSPARQL CRS IRI, or WGS84 when there is none). The geometry map component reads them from the page and reprojects them in the browser. The server does no conversion, and the map needs no follow-up request. → FR-HTML-07.
  4. Template. A template per URI template or resource type, falling back to the generic subject page, writes Flux markup with the content inside the tags (in the light DOM or in slots), so that the page is readable without JavaScript. → FR-HTML-03, NFR-UI-01, NFR-UI-04, Design system: Flux. The template engine is open question 9.
  5. Interactive parts are placeholders that the browser fills later, with follow-up requests (see below): incoming relations, trees, collection tables, and the map's interaction.

docs.title: Response headers
docs.text: Header When Value Requirement Content-Type always the negotiated media type FR-CN-01 Content-Language HTML the chosen interface language FR-HTML-12 Vary when the format, profile or language was negotiated from headers Accept, Accept-Profile, Accept-Language (HTML, when no ?lang= is given) and, in phase 2, Authorization. Omitted for a suffix or _format, whose URL already fixes the format FR-CN-06, NFR-SEC-03 Content-Location when negotiated the format-specific URL, for example /doc/x.ttl FR-CN-02, FR-CN-07 Link always rel="alternate" per format and profile, and per other distribution with a media type; rel="profile" for the profile used; rel="describedby" to the domain's dataset description (ADR 0019); rel="collection" to the event stream that publishes the resource, where configured (ADR 0023) FR-CN-03, FR-CN-04, FR-ES-01, FR-META-01 ETag, Cache-Control 200 and 304 a weak tag (W/"…"): a short hash of the tenant's data version, its configuration version, the SPieGeL version and the variant (media type, profile, language), so that a rollout without new data still changes it (ADR 0020); Cache-Control follows the fixed lifetime only as a fallback. private for non-public access levels; for public responses a short max-age of minutes, then revalidation NFR-OPS-03, NFR-SEC-03, NFR-PRIV-03 Access-Control-Allow-Origin public responses *. Credentialed requests follow normal CORS rules NFR-OPEN-01 Content-Security-Policy HTML as strict as Flux allows NFR-UI-03 X-Robots-Tag responses to authenticated callers noindex FR-HTML-16

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Every error is an HTML page for a browser and application/problem+json for any other client, with the type IRI named below under https://w3id.org/spiegel/problem/ (ADR 0016, FR-CN-10).

Situation Status Note E1. Unknown host, no matching template, or a resource that does not exist or may not be seen 404 One answer for all of these (NFR-SEC-07). HTML through vl-http-error-message. Problem type not-found. E2. Data source error 502 Nothing is cached. The body does not include the store's error message or the query text. Problem type source-error. E3. Data source timeout 504 As E2. Problem type source-timeout. E4. Pool or queue full for a data source 503 with Retry-After NFR-OPS-02. Concerns the service as a whole, unlike E7. Problem type overloaded. E5. No acceptable media type 406 FR-CN-05. Problem type not-acceptable. E6. Requested profile not available 200 with the default profile Allowed by Content Negotiation by Profile. The Link header names the profile actually used. E7. Client over its rate limit 429 with Retry-After NFR-OPS-08. Checked at step 3a, before any query. Unlike 503, it concerns one client, not the service. Problem type rate-limited.

docs.title: /sparql
docs.text:
1. Steps 1 to 3a as above: receive, resolve the tenant, identify the caller, and check the rate limit, which is stricter for /sparql (NFR-OPS-08).
  2. Read the query from query (GET, or a POST form) or from a POST body of type application/sparql-query. A request without a query gets, by content negotiation, the SPARQL Service Description in an RDF format (FR-META-03), or for a browser the HTML editor opened on the tenant's default query (FR-SPARQL-03, FR-SPARQL-04).
  3. Check it against the query policy. RunSparqlQuery passes the query to the QueryInspector, which parses it with strict SPARQL 1.1 syntax, knowing the tenant's prefixes. An update fails as a parse error. Anything other than SELECT, CONSTRUCT, ASK or DESCRIBE, and any SERVICE, is rejected with 400. Graphs are not checked: the store's account for the level decides what is visible. This is defence in depth: read-only access is guaranteed by the store's credentials (NFR-SEC-01). See ADR 0011. Besides any violations, the inspector returns the query form, which the next step needs.

  4. Negotiate the result format, before the query runs. Accept is weighed against the formats of the query form (FR-SPARQL-02):

    Query form Formats Default SELECT, ASK application/sparql-results+json, application/sparql-results+xml, text/csv, text/tab-separated-values; an HTML table with clickable IRIs for browsers (FR-SPARQL-03) SPARQL JSON CONSTRUCT, DESCRIBE text/turtle, application/ld+json, application/rdf+xml, application/n-triples; HTML for browsers Turtle

    No acceptable format for this form gives 406 (not-acceptable), and the store is not queried. A client that does not know the form in advance can accept both kinds, for example application/sparql-results+json, text/turtle;q=0.9. 5. Run it on the data source the tenant names for /sparql (by default its triple store; an Ontop source for a tenant whose data is only relational), with the credentials for the caller's access level, within the same bounded pool, and with a timeout and a result limit (FR-AC-03, NFR-OPS-02). The store gets the query unchanged, but not the caller's Accept. The SPARQL adapter asks the store for a fixed format that it reads as a stream, such as N-Triples for graphs and SPARQL JSON for results. SPieGeL therefore offers the same formats on every store, can count against the result limit, and never passes on the store's own error bodies (ADR 0016). 6. Serialise and respond. The core neither holds nor writes the results (ADR 0010). RunSparqlQuery returns a handle from the SPARQL adapter that writes the results, as they arrive, in the negotiated media type to the response. CSV, TSV, SPARQL JSON, Turtle and N-Triples are streamed; JSON-LD and RDF/XML are written once the result is complete, within the result limit. JSON-LD from CONSTRUCT and DESCRIBE follows the JSON-LD profile parameter: without one, or with compacted, it is compacted with the tenant's context (ADR 0017); expanded and flattened are written as asked, without context (ADR 0024). A frame does not apply, because the result has no single subject. The response has Vary: Accept and CORS for public use (NFR-OPEN-01), and is not cached by default. A timeout gives 504 (source-timeout).

docs.title: Follow-up requests from the browser
docs.text:
The interactive components (incoming relations, the hierarchy, the collection table) request more data after the page has loaded. A map of the resource's own geometries does not: its data is already in the page.

They request paged lists, which are Linked Data resources in their own right (ADR 0015): ?_property=… for the values of a property of the subject, ?_inverse=… for the resources that refer to it through one predicate, and ?_inverse alone for the overview of incoming predicates with a bounded count each. A component asks for JSON-LD with SPieGeL's fixed @context; a harvester can ask for the same list in Turtle. Each page is described with Hydra and links to the next one, so no total is needed.

A list follows the same steps as dereferencing: tenant, identity, rate limit, cache under the data version with the access level in the key, and bounded queries with LIMIT N+1. Its queries are SPieGeL's default templates or the tenant's own QuerySpecs. Nothing is queried through /sparql from the browser.

docs.title: Front page and keyword search
docs.text:
• Front page (FR-HTML-02, FR-HTML-09): GET / on a tenant's host name. Steps 1 and 2 select the tenant from the host, so every host name, such as data.imjv.omgeving.vlaanderen.be or data.bodemenondergrond.vlaanderen.be, gets its own front page. The page is built from discovery blocks: the tenant's block queries (by default DCAT catalogues with their datasets, SKOS concept schemes, and rdfs:Class and owl:Class) run like any QuerySpec, at the public access level, bounded, with a timeout, and cached (steps 9 to 13). The template renders the non-empty blocks after an optional configured introduction, example queries and search terms. If one block fails, the page shows the other blocks and says that one could not be loaded. Unlike a resource description, a front page is a list of independent blocks. An unknown host gets 404, as in step 2.
  • Portal page (FR-HTML-08): the front page of the umbrella tenant (algemeen) also lists every published domain and links to its front page. The list is discovered from the tenant configuration (all tenants), from the actual publication (a query on the umbrella domain's open data catalogue), or from both, merged with configured entries for domains published elsewhere. Which source is used is open question 25.
  • Keyword search (FR-SRCH-01): steps 1 to 3, then two queries through the search port (a count, then a page of results) with the same bounds and timeouts, rendered as a list. Whether it stays is open question 4.

docs.title: Choices this chapter makes
docs.text:
These follow from the requirements, but deserve confirmation in an ADR when the code is written:

  • The 303 does not check whether the resource exists (step 5).
  • A failed or timed-out query makes the request fail, never a partial page. A description cut off at the ceiling is served, but always marked as incomplete (step 12, NFR-OPS-09).
  • Labels for HTML come from a query declared by the HTML profile (rendering step 1).

Related decisions: edge concerns (ADR 0022), default and hand-written queries (ADR 0012). Related open question: presentation rules (21).

docs.title: Implementation Plan: Feature 001, Dereference a resource as RDF
docs.text: Spec: docs/specs/001-dereference-resource-as-rdf/spec.md Decisions: ADR 0004, 0010, 0011, 0012, 0013, 0016, 0018 (docs/adr/) Created: 2026-10-26

docs.title: Context
docs.text: SPieGeL is still an empty skeleton: six Maven modules with only package-info.java, AccessLevel and an ArchitectureTest. Spec 001 (approved) asks for the walking skeleton of phase 1: an id URI answers 303 to its doc URI, and a doc URI returns the bounded description of the thing in Turtle, N-Triples, RDF/XML or JSON-LD, with problem details for every error. Everything comes from a tenant configuration in Turtle; nothing is specific to a domain. This plan builds the first path through core, configuration adapter, SPARQL adapter, web adapter and application.

docs.title: Global Constraints
docs.text:
• All code, comments, identifiers, log and error messages and test names in British English (CLAUDE.md).
  • Java 21, Spring Boot 4.1.1, Apache Jena 6.2.0 (ADR 0004). No new runtime dependencies other than jena-core (core), jena-arq (web, sparql), jena-shacl (config).
  • The core depends on jena-core only, never on org.apache.jena.sparql.., query.., riot.., http.., rdflink.., Spring or servlet APIs (ADR 0010, NFR-Q-01). Adapters never depend on each other.
  • Values from a request enter a query only as bound terms, never as text (NFR-SEC-04).
  • Every IRI and URL that is used or sent comes from the domain's configured base, never from the request (FR-1).
  • Problem types under https://w3id.org/spiegel/problem/: not-found 404, not-acceptable 406, invalid-request 400, method-not-allowed 405, source-error 502, source-timeout 504, internal-error 500 (ADR 0016).
  • Cache-Control: no-store on every 5xx. No store message, stack trace or query text in an error body.
  • Every response carries Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and exposes Link, Location, Content-Location.
  • Logs: one structured entry per request, with request identifier, status and duration; no IP address, no query values other than _format (NFR-PRIV-02).
  • Defaults: blank-node depth 3, time-out per data source 10 seconds (AC-5.5).
  • Requirement IDs are never renumbered. Each test class names the AC or FR it covers in @DisplayName, as AccessLevelTest does.

docs.title: Decisions made while planning
docs.text:
These follow from the spec and the ADRs, and were confirmed with the user where they touch the public configuration vocabulary.

  1. spiegel:base (one IRI, such as <https://data.example.org>) replaces spiegel:hostName from the sketch in ADR 0012. It gives scheme and host together; the host name used to resolve the tenant is taken from it.
  2. Every spiegel:ResourceType declares both api:itemTemplate and api:uriTemplate, with the same variables. The exception for /doc/emissie/{id} therefore also names /id/emissie/{id}.
  3. spiegel:timeout (xsd:duration) is set on a spiegel:DataSource in the tenant Turtle, default PT10S; spiegel:blankNodeDepth on the tenant, default 3.
  4. A query names its data source with spiegel:dataSource; without one it runs on the tenant's spiegel:defaultDataSource, which is required.
  5. SPieGeL's default description query is generated for the configured depth by the configuration adapter: a CONSTRUCT with one UNION branch per level for the node's own triples and one for the label and type of its IRI objects. It was tried on Jena 6.2 with a chain of four blank nodes: levels 1 to 3 are returned, level 4 appears only as an object, and incoming links are absent.
  6. The core bounds every description, whatever query produced it (DescriptionBounds): the subject's triples, blank nodes to the depth, and only label and type of linked IRIs. AC-2.2 to AC-2.4 therefore hold for tenant queries too.
  7. SERVICE is found by walking the algebra (Algebra.compile and Walker.walk), not with ElementWalker: a test on Jena 6.2 showed that ElementWalker misses SERVICE inside FILTER EXISTS, while the algebra walk finds it in subqueries, EXISTS, NOT EXISTS, BIND and select expressions. ADR 0011, decision 2, is amended to say so.
  8. A raw path segment must consist of URI characters only (unreserved, sub-delims, :, @, percent-encoding). A test showed that Jena's substitution writes an IRI containing > unescaped, so a segment such as a%3E is matched on its decoded value but the IRI is built from the raw, still-encoded segment.
  9. Descriptions are serialised to a byte array before the status is sent. That makes the RDF/XML check and "never 200 then fail" simple; streaming arrives with the size ceiling of feature 002.
  10. RDF serialisation stays in the web adapter with Jena RIOT. A RendererPort is introduced with HTML in feature 005, when a second renderer exists (Anti-Abstraction Gate).

docs.title: Pre-implementation gates
docs.text:
• Simplicity: the feature touches the four existing modules that phase 1 provides plus the application; no new module. One new dependency per adapter, all from Jena, which ADR 0004 and 0010 already chose. No caching, pools or limits (feature 002).
  • Anti-abstraction: Spring MVC, Jena RIOT, Jena SHACL and Jena's HTTP query execution are used directly. Ports exist only where the hexagonal design requires them (DataSourcePort, QueryInspector, TenantConfigurationPort). One model: the core's records; no DTOs.
  • Integration first: Phase 0 writes the HTTP contract (contracts/api.md) and an end-to-end contract test per acceptance criterion, before any production code.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: A running SPieGeL that, from one tenant configuration in Turtle and a SPARQL endpoint, answers id URIs with 303, doc URIs with a bounded description in four RDF formats, and every error with problem details.

docs.title: Phase 0: Contracts and tests first
docs.text:
Implements: FR-1 to FR-4 (as contract) | Satisfies: writes the failing end-to-end test for AC-1.1 to AC-1.4, AC-1.6, AC-2.1 to AC-2.8, AC-3.1 to AC-3.16, AC-4.1 to AC-4.6 Files: pom.xml, spiegel-core/pom.xml, spiegel-adapter-sparql/pom.xml, spiegel-adapter-config/pom.xml, spiegel-adapter-web/pom.xml, spiegel-app/pom.xml, spiegel-app/src/test/java/.../ArchitectureTest.java, spiegel-adapter-sparql/src/test/java/be/vlaanderen/omgeving/spiegel/adapter/sparql/testing/StubSparqlEndpoint.java, spiegel-app/src/test/java/be/vlaanderen/omgeving/spiegel/ContractTenant.java, spiegel-app/src/test/resources/contract-data.ttl, spiegel-app/src/test/java/be/vlaanderen/omgeving/spiegel/DereferenceContractTest.java, docs/specs/001-dereference-resource-as-rdf/contracts/api.md Interfaces: Consumes: nothing. Produces: StubSparqlEndpoint.serving(Graph), .servingAfter(Graph, Duration), .failing(), .slow(Duration), .url(), .requestCount(), .close() (test-jar of spiegel-adapter-sparql); ContractTenant.write(Path, String main, String second, String failing, String slow); the HTTP contract in contracts/api.md.

Lock down the HTTP behaviour and the build before any production code: dependencies per ADR 0010, the extra architecture rule, a stub SPARQL endpoint that every later phase reuses, and one end-to-end test per acceptance criterion that runs against the whole application.

  • [ ] Parent pom.xml: add to <dependencyManagement>

  <version>${jena.version}</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>

  <version>${jena.version}</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>be.vlaanderen.omgeving.spiegel</groupId>

package be.vlaanderen.omgeving.spiegel.adapter.sparql.testing;

import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpExchange;
import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer;
import java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.UncheckedIOException;
import java.net.InetSocketAddress;
import java.net.URLDecoder;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import org.apache.jena.graph.Graph;
import org.apache.jena.query.Query;
import org.apache.jena.query.QueryFactory;
import org.apache.jena.riot.Lang;
import org.apache.jena.riot.RDFWriter;
import org.apache.jena.sparql.exec.QueryExec;

/**
 * A SPARQL endpoint for tests: answers {@code CONSTRUCT} and {@code DESCRIBE} queries on an
 * in-memory graph in N-Triples, or fails, or answers too late.
 */
public final class StubSparqlEndpoint implements AutoCloseable {

    /** The message a failing endpoint sends, which must never reach a client. */
    public static final String STORE_MESSAGE = "Virtuoso 37000 Error SP030: internal store detail";

    private final HttpServer server;
    private final AtomicInteger requests = new AtomicInteger();

    private StubSparqlEndpoint(Graph data, boolean fail, Duration delay) {
        try {
            server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress("127.0.0.1", 0), 0);
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new UncheckedIOException(e);
        }
        server.createContext("/sparql", exchange -> answer(exchange, data, fail, delay));
        server.setExecutor(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor());
        server.start();
    }

    public static StubSparqlEndpoint serving(Graph data) {
        return new StubSparqlEndpoint(data, false, Duration.ZERO);
    }

    /** Serves the data, but only after a delay, to measure what SPieGeL adds to a store's time. */
    public static StubSparqlEndpoint servingAfter(Graph data, Duration delay) {
        return new StubSparqlEndpoint(data, false, delay);
    }

    public static StubSparqlEndpoint failing() {
        return new StubSparqlEndpoint(null, true, Duration.ZERO);
    }

    public static StubSparqlEndpoint slow(Duration delay) {
        return new StubSparqlEndpoint(null, false, delay);
    }

    public String url() {
        return "http://127.0.0.1:" + server.getAddress().getPort() + "/sparql";
    }

    /** The number of queries received so far. */
    public int requestCount() {
        return requests.get();
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        server.stop(0);
    }

    private void answer(HttpExchange exchange, Graph data, boolean fail, Duration delay) throws IOException {
        requests.incrementAndGet();
        try (exchange) {
            if (!delay.isZero()) {
                Thread.sleep(delay);
            }
            if (fail || data == null) {
                send(exchange, 500, "text/plain", STORE_MESSAGE.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
                return;
            }
            Query query = QueryFactory.create(queryText(exchange));
            QueryExec exec = QueryExec.graph(data).query(query).build();
            Graph result = query.isDescribeType() ? exec.describe() : exec.construct();
            var body = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
            RDFWriter.source(result).lang(Lang.NTRIPLES).output(body);
            send(exchange, 200, "application/n-triples", body.toByteArray());
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }

    private static String queryText(HttpExchange exchange) throws IOException {
        String form = "GET".equals(exchange.getRequestMethod())
                ? exchange.getRequestURI().getRawQuery()
                : new String(exchange.getRequestBody().readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        String contentType = exchange.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("Content-Type");
        if (contentType != null && contentType.startsWith("application/sparql-query")) {
            return form;
        }
        for (String pair : form.split("&")) {
            if (pair.startsWith("query=")) {
                return URLDecoder.decode(pair.substring("query=".length()), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            }
        }
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("no query parameter");
    }

    private static void send(HttpExchange exchange, int status, String type, byte[] body) throws IOException {
        exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Content-Type", type);
        exchange.sendResponseHeaders(status, body.length);
        exchange.getResponseBody().write(body);
    }
}

    }

        Files.createDirectories(dir.resolve("queries"));
        Files.writeString(dir.resolve("tenant.ttl").toAbsolutePath(), """
                @prefix spiegel: <https://w3id.org/spiegel/config#> .
                @prefix api:     <http://purl.org/linked-data/api/vocab#> .
                @prefix sh:      <http://www.w3.org/ns/shacl#> .
                @prefix xsd:     <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

                <#tenant> a spiegel:Tenant ;
                    spiegel:base <https://data.example.org> ;
                    spiegel:defaultDataSource <#main> ;
                    spiegel:resourceType <#generic>, <#emissie>, <#vestiging>, <#fout>, <#traag> .

                <#main>    a spiegel:DataSource ; spiegel:endpoint <%s> .
                <#second>  a spiegel:DataSource ; spiegel:endpoint <%s> .
                <#failing> a spiegel:DataSource ; spiegel:endpoint <%s> .
                <#slow>    a spiegel:DataSource ; spiegel:endpoint <%s> ;
                    spiegel:timeout "PT1S"^^xsd:duration .

                <#generic> a spiegel:ResourceType ;
                    api:itemTemplate "/id/{concept}/{id}" ;
                    api:uriTemplate  "/doc/{concept}/{id}" ;
                    spiegel:variable [ spiegel:name "concept" ; sh:pattern "^[a-z]+$" ] ,
                                     [ spiegel:name "id" ; sh:pattern "^[0-9]+$" ] .

                <#emissie> a spiegel:ResourceType ;
                    api:itemTemplate "/id/emissie/{id}" ;

                <#vestiging> a spiegel:ResourceType ;
                    api:itemTemplate "/id/vestiging/{id}" ;
                    api:uriTemplate  "/doc/vestiging/{id}" ;
                    spiegel:query [ spiegel:file "queries/describe.rq" ] ,
                                  [ spiegel:file "queries/describe.rq" ; spiegel:dataSource <#second> ] .

                <#fout> a spiegel:ResourceType ;
                    api:itemTemplate "/id/fout/{id}" ;
                    api:uriTemplate  "/doc/fout/{id}" ;
                    spiegel:query [ spiegel:file "queries/describe.rq" ] ,
                                  [ spiegel:file "queries/describe.rq" ; spiegel:dataSource <#failing> ] .

                <#traag> a spiegel:ResourceType ;
                    api:itemTemplate "/id/traag/{id}" ;
                    api:uriTemplate  "/doc/traag/{id}" ;
                    spiegel:query [ spiegel:file "queries/describe.rq" ; spiegel:dataSource <#slow> ] .
                """.formatted(main, second, failing, slow));
        Files.writeString(dir.resolve("queries/describe.rq"), """

        Files.writeString(dir.resolve("queries/emissie.rq"), """
                CONSTRUCT { ?resource ?p ?o . ?resource <https://example.org/ns/viaQuery> "emissie" }
                WHERE { ?resource ?p ?o }
                """);
        return dir;
    }
}

        void methodNotAllowed(String method) throws Exception {

    private ResultActions expectProblem(ResultActions actions, int status, String type) throws Exception {
        return actions.andExpect(status().is(status))
                .andExpect(content().contentType("application/problem+json"))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.type").value(PROBLEM + type))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.status").value(status))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.instance").value(startsWith("urn:uuid:")));

    private Graph turtle(String url) throws Exception {
        MvcResult r = mvc.perform(get(url).header("Accept", "text/turtle")).andExpect(status().isOk()).andReturn();
        return parse(r, "TURTLE");

        Lang l = org.apache.jena.riot.RDFLanguages.nameToLang(lang);
        return RDFParser.fromString(r.getResponse().getContentAsString(StandardCharsets.UTF_8), l).toGraph();
    }

    private static Graph load(String resource) {
        return RDFParser.source(DereferenceContractTest.class.getResource(resource).toString()).toGraph();
    }

    private static Node iri(String iri) {
        return NodeFactory.createURI(iri);
    }
